HOW THE -POOR LIVE. BIT AARON WATSON. East to West was crying, crying : "Of God's mercy, give us room! We are homeless, we are outcast, We are crowded nigh to death! All your life is full af sunshine; Ours is darker than the tomb. Mercy give us space to live in; give us breath." London heard the cry and shudder'd. "Who are these who call for space? Who are those whose million voices Rise and mingle into one? God has laid a burden on them, Or they've linger'd in the race; What to help them, what to save them, can be done ?" Piety, with tears and blessings, Wealth, with money in its palms, Went through slum, and court, and alley. "It is sad and true," they said. Sympathy, its heart awaken'd, Bountifully scattered alms; Yet the living still were crowded like the dead. So the cry grew louder, stronger, Till At length all England heard— " Tis not charity we ask for; OfaGod's mercy, give us room And at last the cold and callous Heart'of Parliament was stirred; "We must try," it said, "to save them from theif doom."

Dukes, and Marquises, and Barons, Ye who sit in gilded places— Ye, too, whom a trusting country Called to plan and mould its laws— Ye were asking how the poor live! The reply's before your faces, All their misery's unburied, and its cause. There it's written; there's the story! Labour herds in loathsome dens, Huddles into holes and garrets, Swarms from dismal base to roof; Not through God's fault; nor the law's fault; All the awful fault is men's; In the volume now before you lies the proof. Let me state the truth quite briefly— Almost all the words are yours 'Tie not any law that's wanted; Laws have failed, will fail again; Men and women herd together, And are crowded to the doors, Just through those you wont abolish—Vestrymen. "For some reason or another—" What! you find the truth too plain? Men may covet public office All for greed and this is why, Deeming sacrifice of others Glorious if it end in gain, They have huddled up their fellows till they die. Basest disregard of duty! Basest treachery and fraud! , .2 God is certain to remember What his creatures may forget; And such piling up of riches, Whosoever may applaud. God is sure, at last, to reckon as a debt. London, London, bound and helpless, Like a giant held with bands, Who is this that men must die for? Who is this that binds your strength? Rise; there's majesty within you; There is might within your hands: Rise, and throw the pigmies off at length—at it* length!

Lay not thy heart open to every one; but treat of thy affairs with the wise, and such as fear God.—A-Kempis. The golden moments in the stream of life rush past us, and we see nothing but sand; the angels come to visit us, and we only know them when they are gone.—George

Eliot. Do not grow old too fast. Try to keep your sympathies fresh, and your interest in little things active. Gray hairs and wrinkles you cannot escape, but you need not grow old in feeling unless you choose. An attorney brought in an immense bill to a lady for some business he had done for her. The ladv,lo whom he had once paid his addresses, murmured at ihe.charges. " Madam," replied the limb of the law, "I wanted to convince you that my profession is lucrative, and that I should not have been a bad match." THE BIRTH OF A GREAT WORIL—In the year 1.840, a young lawyer's clerk, living in London, was smitten with coasumption. The doctors told him that it could be arrested "if taken in time"—if he could have perfect rest, pure air, and suitable nourishment. But these luxuries were wholly beyond his own reach. His master, a young solicitor, took a warm interest in his case, and tried to procure his admission into some hospital; but he found every hospital door closed against one suffering from the early (and only hopeful) stage of this malady. Such was not "a suitable subject" for their help. The young lawyer, with indomitable energy, then resolved that his clerk should have a hospital of his own, in which he should be the first patient. He called together a few gentlemen, to whose sympathy and aid he appealed, with the result that a little house was opened in a by-street at Chelsea, for the reception of consumptive patients. From that small beginning grew the great Brompton Hospital for Consumption, with its kindred institutions in East London, Bournemouth. and the Isle of Wight. Benefactions and contributions poured in, but on no earthly" subscription list" can be registered the suffer- ing of that forlorn young clerk, which was really the Moses' rod which struck the rock of human regardless- mess, and let forth the waters of refreshment and heal- ing. Surely that suffering was no less allotted to him by his Loving Father in heaven, to be returned for the good of his brethren, than is the wealth which God spares to others that they may be his stewards thereof. And how far may not that poor invalid's benefaction reach? Icor not only has it brought about an asylum for the con- sumptive patient, but thereby—as its managers testify —it nes given an opportunity for the more careful study of this destructive malady and of the laws whose neg- lect leads to it, so that it may be not only shorn of its terrors, but in time—long stretches of time—eradicated altogether. And now, from that incident, accidentally revealed, and probably to be utterly forgotten in the lapse of centuries, let us Item to understand what is never revealed. Let us think of the nameless suffering lives which have inspired songs and stories and sermons, which have borne fruits of help and peaee and joy! It is an endless vista which opens.—The Quiver for May. How TO PLEASE AN THISHMAN.—" Poor fellow! It's I not twice a week he gets a dinner," said Father Pant. "He 'got mine once, though I wish it had been a better one for his sake! I was going cif to a sick call—a hur- ried case—and he. knowing all about it, having seen me drive down the Limerick road, marched HD to the house and told Mary Johnston that I had sent him up to bid her give him my dinner. I was gone off to Clifton's, eight miles away—he had his story all pat enough—she believed him, and—Lord Cork made•short work of my dinner !" "Unfortunate wretches!" said the inspector. " What an existence it is! It makes me melancholy to see the crowds of such creatures in all these southern towns." "Yes," added the doctor, "and the crowds of young ones growing up to the trade." "Well, well," observed the inspector, "the schools should see to that, but the managers are in fault. Now, at Newstown last summer—l went to Newstown to inspect a National school—l recollect it well—it was a lovely July day—l Sound the door of the boys' school locked, and of all the pandemoniums ever you listened to, it sounded through the windows. At last some of the urchins heard me and spoke to me through a broken pane of glass. 'Where's the teacher?' I asked. 'Plase, your honour, he's gone up to the manager's to help in with the hay, and we're all locked in till he comes back.' After this I went to the girls' school. That was impracticable also, and a buzz, not exactly that of bees, came to my ears. Where is the mistress?' I hailed at last. Flue, your honour, she's gone up to the manager's to give a band with the washing, and she's locked us in till she comes back.' " Oh, scandalous," said Father Paul. "Very well, but listen to this ?" continued the inspector. "Sly duty as inspector was to direct the said manager's attention to this state of things; and request him to see that it did not occur again." "And it vras the manager who was the cause of it," said the doctor. "That matches the old schoolmaster and his plan when they were about to introduce the National school system. It's close on forty year's since. There were a number of gentlemen going about the country taking evidence; among others they fell in with an ota schoolmaster in my part of Waterford, and they asked his opinion, would the people like a free school or a pay school best." 'Oh! he said, they would not like a free school at all. They are too proud, too proud entirely for that!' Oh ! then we had better arrange to make them pay something,' said these Cornelis- sioners. Oh no, then, replied the schoolmaster. That won't do; they would object to pay either!' What does this mean,' cried the gentlemen, since von are after telling us they were too proud to send their chil- dren to a free school?' That is so, too!' said the schoolmaster. And what do you mean?' they cried. What are we to do ?" Well I'he made answer, have an idea of what it is that they would like, and what it is would suit them—myself, just!' Tell us, if you please,' said the commissioners, they all being mightily puzzled. 'lt is this, then, just—to make a fixed charge, moderate like, not too moderate; and then when the time came to pay, to not ask them to pay! not to press them to pay any- thing at all—just leave it to them. like !' " Father Paul laughed his great deep-chested laugh that made the whole room shake. "You invented that, you villain— you made that up," he said, at last. "I give you my word of honour it is just what happened, sir !" replied the doctor. TO PARTIES ABOUT TO HOLIDAY.

The reader is not to conclude that the writer heieoi intends stealing Punch's advice to parties about to marry, "1)0/Irl';" on the contrary, he would say, most emphatically, "DO" by all means. This advice may be regarded as superfluous by such parties, but there is rather a lengthy postscript attached, and this P.S. is of the greatest importance to the parties concerned; in fact, this superfluous advice may be likened to the spoonful of jam administered in our unsuspecting youth, and the postcript can play the part of the pill which was always ingeniously concealed therein. And it is the earnest wish of the writer that this metaphori- cal pill may not share the fate of the material and more mysterious compound and be "spit out" after the jam has been swallowed, but that it will be given a fair chance of purging the moral nature of the party on whose account it has been manufactured. Now, from time immemorial (or thereabouts) parties about to holi- day have always considered a good guide book, a knap- sack, an alpenstock, or some such nonsense, the prin- cipal requisites for a tour; therefore, be it known by these presents that the most important things are : (1) a stock of good temper, guaranteed to wear like pin- wire all through the holiday, and calculated to make honey turn yellow with envy at it sweetness; and (2) a stock of £s. d. Ladies will find No. 1 particularly handy when witnessing the ruination of the paper bag containing their best bonnet, and No. 2—well, No. 2 is always handy, but especially to the aforesaid lady if she wishes to reward the careless porter. In calculating ex- penses before starting, all parties should multiply by three their first estimate for extras, as many a holiday has been brought to an untimely conclusion in conse- sequence of the disregard paid to this simple sum in arithmetic. Parties must make up their minds that they will not be cheeseparing in any way (not even with the German bands) ; this will save haggling when engaging apartments. But why haggle? You go to the seaside, with your wife and small family, when it is crowded; you are asked perhaps a couple of guineas per week for a double-bedded room, and double that amount for a sitting-room; you impertinently remark (though you think it witty) that you don't wish to purchase the house and furniture, so you very properly get the door slammed in your face, and it serves you, sir, jolly well right if you have to spend the night in a bathing machine, though we pity your wife and small family in having such a husband and father. Just consider the whole thing in a different light. Some medical gentleman of superhuman insight discovers that a certain little village which has never figured in any topographical dictionary is the healthiest spot in Great Britain; fine bay, breezes from the west, &c. Or it may be a delightful corner in North Wales, with enchanting waterfalls, high mountains, pretty lake,—anything you like. This discovery gets into the newspapers of course. (And you, sir, who spent the night in the bathing machine, are at liberty to think the aforesaid medical gentleman was bribed by the Local Board orthe property owners of the respective districts. I am not going to waste time arguing with you.) Paterfamilias reads this in the papers and says," 11l take the old woman and the youngsters down there for a month." Almost simultaneously a great number of other people have said the same thing, and they go—all of them! But where are they to atop? Hotels and lodging-houses are built solely for their benefit, and the residents spend their savings in furniture, and hope by hard work in the sea- so (and a bit of fishing during the winter months) to earn a living. It is quite true that they have only some three months work, but what work it is,—it is nothing less than downright slavery! And you, sir, whom we have relegated to the bathing machine, how dare you grumble at a perfectly reasonable charge, you who pay £2OO per annum for your house rent, and an average of £2O for each of your servants! Parties will do well to recollect that it is not safe to I carry on a conversation at the top of the voice with other parties, some two hundred yards distant, on a crowded promenade. The writer once heard something like the following when at Darkpool, and everybody Iwithin earshot knew where the parties hailed from. Scene, crowded promenade, parties far apart : " Whooa dosta think's gettten wed this morning?" " Whorr " Whoa's ta think's getten wed?" " Heaw the —dooali know!" " Tum-o'-Dick-o'-Tum-o'-RucLuts !" "The —he hez ! Who the her he getten howd on 2" Whorr ?" " Whoa's thad gotten?' ' "Well ahll be Parties should on no account let the folks at home know their holiday address. When you've got up early stlmuch inconvenience for the purpose ot getting up Snowdon, what could be more agonising than the receipt of a letter from home containing, amongst other items, the cheerful intelligence that Jones has put you in the County Court for the very suit you are touring in— that you have 'test 7d. in discount through not paying your gas bill before starting, and that Johnny fell down- stairs yesterday and knocked several teeth out. It is small things of this sort which cause a man to forego the necessary bottle of beer on reaching the top of the mountain. Parties of young men should endeavour not to bring disgrace upon the districts from which they hail by everlastingly making bad puns when on their holidays; a little exuberance is excusable, but they should re- member that even the Welsh understand English, and to exßect them to survive the eternal repetition of puns to which their remote ancestors listened in the time of Noah is surely, expecting too much. The, repetition of the antiquated joke that Snowdon is so called simply because it is snowed on is overlooked if the party re- peating it is an imbecile, but there is no such thing as overlooking an attempted pun on the name of the pretty village of Pwllygwgallywchnog!!! No! boiling oil is too good for the wretch who would be so inhuman. To conclude, don't go to places merely that you may brag about having been there; don't make yourself into a globe-trotter. Go away with a fixed purpose to see all that is to be seen, and to see it well; to get all the bene- fit to be got from such a holiday; to have a real good time of it generally, and, lastly, don't omit to paste a copy of these rules by the side of the little mirror in your hat. Jos. B—.

- - 'WARRINGTON DISTRICT HIGHWAY ' BOARD. A general meeting of the members of this B oard was held. on Wednesdiiy afternoon at the 'surfeyoilB4 office, Sankey-st., Warrington. The following mem- bers were present :—Messrs Robert Houghton (in the chair).. T. E.,Withington, J. Hartley,W.Royston, John Fairclough, George Lawton, Henry Bate, Philip I. Bate, Samuel Bent, George A. Caldwell,' Reginald Owen, junr., James Houghton, John Grounds, andl.Pennington, with Messrs H. B. White (law clerk) and Thompson (surveyor).—Mr. Robert Houghton was re-elected chairman of the Board for the ensuing year, Mr. Joseph Hartley was re-elected senior vice-chairman, and Mr. Wil- liam Royston was re-elected junior vice-chairman. The Finance and General Purposes Committee wasi re-appointed, Mr. George A. Caldwell being elected to fill a vacancy caused on the committee by, ;the death of Mr. James Harrison, one of the members.— It was reported that at a special meting of the Finance Committee the surveyor stated that Mr. William Bennett had agreed to let the Board have 180 square yards, for the purposes of widening Pad- gate-road, for .£l5, on certain conditions. The total cost to be incurred would be from £6O to £7O. The committee decided that the offer be accepted, and that the surveyor be instructed to get an agree- ment signed with Mr. William Bennett, and such action was 'now approved by the " Board.— The CLERK reported that on the 14th inst. the balance in the bank amounted to £175 5s 6d.—Esti- mates for the coining year were approved. The fol- lowing is a summary of them :—Ordinarymainten- ance of district roads, £1,700; ordinary maintenance of main roads, £1,550; improvements, £1,041; salaries, .f 320 geneial •expenses, £150; general working balance, £200; making a gross total of £4,961. After allowing for a balance in hand, ;the sum of £3,900 4s 8d waa required to be raised, td do which it was decided to lay a rate ef 8d in the X, throughout the district, at four calls to be Made payable June, August, November, and January. The £1,041 put down for improvements was apportioned amongst the various townships as follows :—Burton- wood £9O, Cuerdley .£3O, Culcheth .E9O, Great Sankey £240., Houghton £l6, Kenyon .£35, Lowton .f4O, Penketh'.£4o, Poulton .£lBO, Rixton £3O, Croft £6O, Winwick £6O, Woolston £3O, Warrington (extra municipal) £loo.—This was the principal business.

A ZULU WARRIOR IN TROUBLE AT WIDNES. On Saturday, at Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Day, Daniel Gilmore, 33 years of age, a fire- man, was charged With having, at Widnes, on the 25th March, feloniously inflicted grievous bodily harm upon Joseph Donovan, with intent to murder him. The prisoner was defended by Mr. Seger. Elie case for the prosecutor—which was conducted by Mr. Shee and Air. Cooper—was that the prisoner, who lived in Barnest., Widnes. suspected Donovan, litho lived next door, of improper conduct with his wife and others. On the 25th March prisoner tpet the prosecutor, and told him that Mrs. Gilmore must not go into the prosecutor's house anymore, as it would only lead to drunkenness and misconduct. About eight o'clock the same Right the prisoner, who was the worse for drink, want to the house and threatened to assault Do-tovan. He was persuaded to go away, but later on, after having had more drink, he returned, used very abusive language, and threw a bottle at prosecutor's head which,, however, did not strike him. The quarrel then ceased; but subsequently the prisoner again attacked Donovan and struck him on the head many times with a chair, which was broken into pieces. Prosecutor called out to prisoner "Don't kill me ; " but, taking no heed of this, the prisoner, after breaking the chair, attacked prosecutor with his flats and knocked him about the floor. The wounds on the injured man bled profusely, and for several days he was in a dangerous position. When apprehended and charged prisoner said, "I have done it, and I would have hurt hart if I could." As a matter of fact, and it was admitted by the defence, there was no reason whatever for the prisoner's suspicion about the misconduct of the prosecutor.—For the de- fence Mr. Segar did not deny the assault, but pointed out the prisoner had suffered a deal from his head, he hay* had sunstroke when on service abroad. Prisoner had served with distinction in the Zulu and Egyptian wars, and had been decorated with the Victoria Cross and two medals. He was a quiet man when not under the influence of drink, but when in an intoxicated condition he was not responsible for his actions, and on this occa- sion he might have thought he was attacking Zulus. (Laughter.)—The jury found the prisoner guilty of wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm.—His Lordship, in sentencing the prisoner to nine months' im- prisonment with hard labour, said he was sorry to see a manwho had previously had a good character brought in the dock throu,,,h drink.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. THURSDAY • EIGHT. The House of Lords has, by exception, succeeded in providing the fieniation of the Parliamentary week. ,• It was Lord Salisbury began it. -Last Fri- day he, suddenly and without observance of the customary usage of advising the object of his atten- tion, attacked Lord Wolseley for the now famous speech delivered a fortnight earlier at the banquet to Sir John Pender. I happened to be present at the banquet and heard with amazement an officer in active command not only attack the Administra- tion under which he served, but indict the system of Parliamentary government under which England has hitherto moderately prospered. It was not sur- prising to hear, as was disclosed in the course of the debate, that Mr. Stanhope,, on reading a report of this speech, immediately communicated with Lord Wolseley, and protested against the line adopted by him. There, it seemed, the matter rested till Lord Salisbury recurred to the subject in the Lords on Friday, Lord Wolseley taking up the story at Mon- day's sitting ; and in a House crowded from floor to gallery, defended his indiscretion. The proceedings in the House of Lords cannot, from the rational point of view, be regarded ,as gtisfactory. .In brief, Lord Wolseley stuck to his guns, and if he is right the country is practically in a defenceless condition by sea and by land. Lord Salisbury made haste to patch up the difference with" Our only General," protesting that his half- threatened resignation would be a blow which the country could ill stand, and there the matter was left. On the whole, the nation has taken this startling exposure of its unprotected condition with marvellous equanimity, varied by a disposition to back up Lord Wolseley. The fact is, that the scare now being got up is one ot a familiar series. When Mr. NV ard Hunt took cirrge of the navy, in 1874, he one night confidentially informed the House that Our national defences were composed of "Ships that could not swim, and soldiers who could not march." We had a paper fleet, and no guns worth speaking of. This raised such a storm, that poor Mr. Ward Hunt, never a very adroit man, bad [urn-

_ - Wringly to 'withdraw. Since then the scare has been recurrent, and is upon us again. Where there is so much smoke there must be fire, and the pro- bability is that Lord Wolseley will have done a conspicuous service by forcing the hand of the military authorities and compelling them to carry out those reforms of administration which appear to be urgently needed. In the debate in the Lords the Duke of Cambridge supplied that touch of comedy which is necessary to the perfect success of the serious drama. On one who had not the good fortune to be present on Fri- day night can realise the delicious humour of the incident by which the portly Duke introduced him- self into the controversy. On Friday there appeared in the " Daily , Telegraph" one of its periodical screeds in which all the floating gossip as to the state of the Army and Navy was collected, boiled down, and set forth in large type upon the highest military authority. "My lords," said the Duke of Cambridge. looking round with inflamed visage and gasping for breath at the enormity of the assumption on the part of the "Daily Tele- graph; "Up to the present moment, I thought I was the highest military authority:' It takes a good deal to make the Lords laugh. But this tick- led them immensely, Lord Salisbury silently, chuck- ling for several minutes after the irate Duke had subsided. This could not be bettered. But the Duke was to the fore again on Monday. Lord Wolseley had excused himself for not taking part in debates in the House of Lords in presence of his military chief " the illustrious duke." The illus- trious duke swallowed this cunningly baited hook, and, amid subdued laughter, effusively commended Lord Wolse!ey for his good sense and right judgment in not venturing to open his mouth on military affairs in the presence of the Commander-in-Chief. The placid and prosperous course of the Govern- ment in the House of Commons has been varied by two incidents. One happened on Monday night, when the King-Harman Salary Bill narrowly escaped defeat in the division lobby; the other, on Wednesday, when Mr. Jesse Collings unwittingly and unwillingly got his dear friends and allies, the Unionist Government in a particularly nasty place. The King-Harnuin Salary Bill is one of those com- paratively small matters which not unfrequently wreck strong Governments. There is no doubt that but for the fixed determination of the Dissentient Liberals to go through any process of humiliation rather than give a vote that would hasten the return to power.of Mr. Gladstone, the Government would have gone out on this measure. As it is, it has preyed a source of ever recurrent trouble. A peen- liaritY about the measure is that,. being a money bill, it must needs go through a double process of consideration in the Commons. It is submitted first in the form of Resolutions, which are read a first time, taken in Committee, reported upon, and then used as a foundation for a bill, which retraces all these steps. Thus the Opposition have had full op- portunity, which, to do them justice, they have fully availed themselves of, till on Monday they were within eight votes of throwing out the bill. ' Wednesday's difficulty, less dramatic in its inci- dent, was not less serious. Mr. Jesse Collings, who, since he left the Liberal ranks, has been going about the country preaching up a Conservative Govern- ment as the true friend of the agricultural labourer, brought in his Small Holdings Bill, apparently hop- ing that the Government and the Conservative party would live up to his description of there. This expectation was only partially fulfilled. Mr. Long, Mr. Chaplain, and others who took part in the debate from the Conservative Bencheswere loud and unanimous in their expressions of sympathy with the agricultural labourer, and of approval of the objects of the measure, attbe same time carefully avoiding a division in which their names would have been recorded in opposition to the bill, a list that might be considered at the General Election. They talked out the bill, leaving Mr. Jesse Collings lamenting. The acuteneSs of the situation was shown in the fact that, for the first time since the Round Table Conference broke up, Mr. Chamberlain voted against the Conservatives. This is a bad time for royalty. The gallant Ger- man Emperor is still fighting hand to hand with death, a struggle the issue of which can be post- poned only for a few weeks, or it may be days. According tc current report. the Czar has just escaped another of the interminable series of attacks upon his life. His potent Majesty, the King of Spain, after undergoing a severe attack of , teething, is now showing signs of a relapse into the hereditary disease of epilepsy. The Emperor of Brazil, it is said, scarcely hopes to see his adopted country again • and now there is news that the King of Holland is already. within the shadow of the valley of death. King William is over three score years and ten, and as far as state affairs are concerned has led a placid. life. But he never got over the blow dealt by the death of the Prince of Orange, which took plaee some nine years ago, the Prince being at the time in the very prime of life. The second son, Alexander, a curious recluse, who was never happy except when he could evade court duties, died five years later, flintiest on the anniver- sary of the death of his eldest brother. This left King William-without a heir to the throne, his only other child being a daughter now in her ninth year. When the Prince of Orange died, the Queen was appointed Regent in casesf emergency, It is pro- bable that before the, year is out we shall find the baby King on the historic throne of Spain ieined hy the Child-Queen ruler Of the Dutch. , In the mean While, out own: gracious sovereign just verging on her seventieth year is in ,uneom- monly good health, and, as those in,immediate' con- nection with the throne complain, in 'ocesSiciiiilly inconvenient vigour. It is purn4te to observe one or two little things seeming to indicate a fixed idea in. her Majesty's mind that her already lengthened reign will be indefinitely prolonged. She has re-
;8 )ed

tdi cently developed quite a mania fkArniialtiOteston- ing, and adding to what Mr. We'rninic4rWizkuld call , her "portable property." When in nominee • she spent a considerable time looking out fee a Site on which to build a residence. This intention is niie finally abandoned; but, as there is plenty of time, it is postponed. The Queen is going to Florence again next year, when the building project will probably agsin come up. Meanwhile Balmoral, the Queen's favourite residence, is being almost rebuilt. A new wing has been added, and the interior of the castle has been re-decorated according to the peculiar German taste of the Queen. Some massive furni- ture has been added, calculated to stand the wear and tear of another twenty years' residence. The announcement that Colonel Tottenham's affairs being wound up, his personalty has been sworn under £648 is a striking and instructive fact. When, nearly a quarter of century ago, he entered Par- liament as member for New Ross, he was the owner of family estates, which brought in £4,000 a year, at that time in Ireland. equal to £6,000 a year on an English rent roll to-day. Ile was at that time a captain in the Scots Guards, and lived much more in London than at Ballyeurry. A tall, remarkably handsome man, he thought that life was given to be enjoyed, and he enjoyed it accordingly. When agricultural depression came, and the tenants found a difficulty in paying the old rents, Colonel Totten- ham insisted upon having his pound of flesh. There was litigation, evictions, and a general process of decay, which ended in Colonel Tottenham dying in New York with £648 Eis his sole possession, ' and Heaven knows what became of the tenants. Messrs. Chatto and. Windus have isstud a verba- tim report of Mr. Whistler's famous "Ten o'clock," the evening's entertainment, which, by way of lec- ture, he had a season or two ago provided for Lon- don. It is beautifully printed on rough white papev, with broad margins and leaves of delightful irregularity of size. It is sown in a cover of brown paper, and is voted "quite the thing." The style is, in some of its flashes, founded' upon that of the old Hebrew prophets, and Mr. Whistler's disap- pointment with Nature is really delicious. "Nature," he graciously admits, "contains the ele- ments in form and colour of all pictures, as the key board contains the notes of all music. But the ar- tist is born to pick and choose, and group with science these elements, that the result may be beau- tiful, as the musician gathers his notes and forms his chords until he brings forth from chaos glorious harmony." That Mr. Whistler's wit is impromptu all his friends know. Take, for example, his retort upon the gushing lady, one of a horde who follow him about and worship him. "There are oxly two painters who live in the world's history," she said to Whistler, "You and Velasquez." "Why drag in Velasquez ?" said Whistler.
THE RECTORSHIP OF WARRINGTON.

THE NEW RECTOR. In a letter received by Messrs. N. B. Percival and . R. W. Francomb, churchwardens of St. Elphin's, the Rev. Frederic .W. Willis, M.A., vicar of All Saints', Wellingborough, Northampton, signifies his accept,- ance of the rectorship of Warrington offered to him by the patron, ,Lord Lilford. The letter runs as follows :

" All Saints' Vicarage, Wellingborough, May 14th, 1888. ." My dear sirs,—l have just heard from Lord Lilford, in reply to my letter, and I lose no time in announcing to you my grateful acceptance of his most kind offer. I do, indeed, feel the intense responsibility, the greatness of the work, and my own unfitness and unworthiness, but I will do my utmost. law sure you will give me your best advice at all times and constant support. Will you kindly make known without delay my decision to all whom it may concern, and tell the parishioners that I earnestly ask for the sympathy and co-operation of all ?—I am, my dear sirs, with many thanks for your courtesy and kindness during my late visit, yours most truly,
" FREDERIC W. WILLIS.

"The churchwarden i of St. Elphin's Parish Church." The new rector' of' Warrington is of Lancashire extraction, having been born near Prescot, and is a brother of a gentleman well known in that locality —Mr. Willis, of Halsmead Park, Whiston. He was educated at Oxford, where he took an M.A. degree. After living a few months at Alderley, Cheshire, the scene of his first curacy, and about 18 months at Rainhill. Mr. Willis was appointed to All Saints, Wellingborough, a living worth .£220. which he holds at the present time. He has in his present , sphere earned the reputation of a hard-working and conscientious clergyman, and Lord Lilford, in a letter to the churchwardens of St. Elphins, says that Mr. Willis has worked with very great success in his present vicarage for about 17 years, and that he has the best rest reasons for believing him emi- nently well qualified forthe important and onerous position of rector of Warrington. ACting under instructions received from the executors of the late Rev. W. Quekett, Mr. Thomas Sutton on Tuesday conducted a sale by auction of the household furniture and effects at the Rectory' There was a large attendance, and the sale lasted about six hours. Over a thousand volumes of mis- cellaneous books were disposed of. The widow of the late Rector, Mrs. Quekett, has left Warrington, and is residing at Eastburne with a relative.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"The Duke's Own, or the Adventures of Peter Daly '' is the title of a capital story by Mr. J. Percy Groves, author of "From Cadet to Captain," "A Soldier Born," &c. Mr. Groves is an experienced soldier as well as story-teller, and his book is there- fore as,instructive as it is interesting. Peter Daly's adventures are wonderfully varied, and they are graphically described, The characters of the story are well drawn and display admirable contrast. There is just so much of history worked into the narrative as to give it backbone and add to the interest. The illustrations, which are altogether Q f a superior kind, are by Lieut.-Col. Marshman. Messrs. Griffith, Farren and Co., are the publishers of "The Duke's Own," and it is due to them to say that the volume is well printed on toned paper, and handsomely bound. It makes an• admirable gift book for boys. The Life'of Victor Hugo by Mr. F. T. Marzials, is published by Mr. Walter Scott,London, as the, current issue of the Great Writers series. This volume furnishes ad interesting and sufficiently full account of the Career of the great Frenchman who is so well known to English readers. There is no blind admiration; Victor Huzo's weakness is 'unveiled as well as his strength ; but, happily for his fame, his failings were few while his,vir- tuesWere many. The reader, after perusing the volume, will be disposed to endorse Mr. Marzials' concluding sen- tence He was one of the world's great poets, and his verse will continue through the after-time as a living force, because, while perfect in workmanship, it is broad-based upon the universal heart, and so eternal."l , In thaCanterbury Poets for May, we have "Smgticle ; poems and lyrics of love's joy and sorrow, by Philip Bourke Marston. Edited with introductory memoir by William Sharp" Although the name of Marston will 1.9 e familiar to most lovers of verso there are comparatively few who have read much of what he has written. This elegant shilling volume will therefore be welcome to the general reader. The life of the young blind poet is a• tale of sorrow ; and it is not surprising to note that I many of his poems are steeped in sadness. But he was a true son of song, and had a poet's keen appreciation of' the beautiful. This is especially seen in the series of, -poems entitled "Garden Secrets,' which are unique in their way. How neatly turned is this stanza : • 0 my garden, full of lilies, White as peace, and very tall, • , In your midst my heart so still is I can hear the least leaf fall. The sonnet,ln the hands of most writers becomes a stiff and formal production; but with Marston it was an easy and natural mode of expression, and the result is that some of his sonnets stand on a level Nith those of Wordsworth, which is the highest praise we Can give.. I "The Morals of Seneca" constitutes the volume of the 1 Camelot issue for May. It is a selection from the prolie writings of the ancient philosopher who has so much in common with Christian doctrine. The volume is edited by Mr. Walter Clode, who gives a summary of the life and times of the teacher who had Nero for a pupil. Nero does not seem to have profited by the wise counsel which was given him, formn the end Seneca became a victim to his cruelty. He died A.D. 65 in his 68th year. He lived, in a great measure, the life he marked out for :himself when he said, in his discourse "on a happy life "-" I will look upon the whole world as my country, and upon the gods both as the witnesses and the judges of my words) and deeds. I will live and die with this testimony—that I loved good studies and a good conscience; that I never invaded another man's liberty, and that I preserved my own."

Chaucer by Professor A. W. Ward is issued by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. in the English Men of Letters, editedl by Mr. John. Morley.. Professor Ward. gives a. pains- taking account of the life and times of the father of Eng- lish poetry. It is a matter of course to say that there is a good deal of uncertainty as to what is the truth about a man who lived over 500 years ago; but many facts are I established and some conjecture is disposed of. The Canterbury Tales, will ever remain the monument of Chaucer's fame. Who can forget his description of the true priest : But Cristei lore and his apostles twelve; He taught, but first he folwed it hiraselve. "The Season " for May is gorgeous with eoloured plates of the latest fashions; and there are no less than 18 illustrated pages of dress and needlework, besides full-sized patterns and designs of embroidery. There are, too, Society notes, and replies to correspondents, all bearing on dress and fashion. " The Season" is issued at Is monthly. • Part 11.2 of Messrs Ward and Locks Technical Journal and Industrial Self-instructor contains, amongst other things, artieles on the general principles of Mechanics, the won-maker, the factory hand, the house planner, thc wood-worker and designer, 'and the venter and his technical work. ' • • • • ' ' • The current issue of the History of Latickshire (part 19) continues the details of the Hundred of Salford. Amongst the more especially interesting illustrations are Salford Cross (taken down in 1824), Old Blackfriars Bridge (taken down in 1820), Radcliffe Hall and the ducking stool, and Old Coffee House and entrance to St. Ann's Square, 1775.

div.head: ST. PETER'S BOUNDARY DISPUTE.
div.p: THE ST. PETER'S BOUNDARY DISPUTE.

It has now been definitely decided to carry out the scheme of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners with regard to an enlargement of St. Peter's parish, Warrington. This decision was announced in the 'following letter :--" Privy Council Office, Whitehall, sth May, 1888. Dear sir,—Referring to your letter of theith March last, and to previous correspon- dence with respect to the scheme of the Ecclesias- tical Commissioners for altering the boundaries of the parish of St. Peter's, Warrington, I am directed by the Lords of the Council to acquaint you that their lordshiPs, having carefully considered all the representations laid before them in relation to the scheme, deemed it their duty to submit the scheme to the Queen for approval, and that her Majesty was pleased to approve of and ratify the said scheme on the 3rd irst.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, C. L PBEL. Wm. Brookes, Esq., Orford Lodge, Warrington." The following is an extract from the order of the Privy Council as published in the "London Gazette," viz:—" The territory?, to be W an- nexed as to the district of St. Peter's, arrington, within the original limits of the parish oi Warring- ton, in the county of Lancaster, and in the diocese of 'Liverpool, being:—All that part of the said parish of Warrington wherein the present incum- bent of such parish now possesses the exclusive cure of souls, which is bounded upon the south-west by the district of St. Peter, Warrington,caforesaid, upon the north-west by the new parish of St. Ann, War- rinLton, within the original limits of the parish of Warrington aforesaid, and upon the remaining side that is to say, upon the east, by an imaginary line commencing upon the boundary which divides the said new parish of St. Ann, Warrington, from the parish of 'Warrington aforesaid, at the poipt ne r Coiiies-corner, where Orford-avenue joins Marsii House-lane, and extending thence eastward along the middle of the said Marsh House-lane for a dis- tance of nearly two chains to its junction with Bat- tersby-lane, and extending thence southward along the middle of the last-named lane for a distance of 28 chains or thereabouts to its junction at the Ches- hire Lines of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway with Brick-st,„ and continuing thence still south- ward along the middle of the said street for a dis- tance of six chains or thereabouts, to the boundary at the junction of the same street with Lythgoes- ; lane, which boundary divides the said parish of Warrington from the 'district of St. Peter, Warring- ', tnn, aforesaid."

CHAPTER XVIIL FOR MY WIFE. A hot July! Such a July as England can seldom boast of, makes London society's queens half in- clined to shut up their }wises, give no more balls, and go to seek open-air amusements among green lanes, or on trimly-cut lawns—when suddenly a rumour is circulated which keeps them all rooted in their town

quarters. Prince Sergius iS•going to give a midnight open-air fete. He has•taken a villa with some lovely grounds at Campden Hill, which, with the assistance of:his marvellous valet, he intends to turn into a fairy land for the evening; and to this fete many Of the grandest and most beautiful of England's daughters are to be _ _

bidden. . "Is it in honour of Irene Stanhope that this thing is done? "' more, than one disappointed mother asks ,of another; for Prince Sergius atten- tions to Miss Stanhope have not failed to be ob- served, and while some few bitter ones aver that he will .return to. Russia without speaking, yet the 1 general idea is that on the night of the great fête he will ask Irene to be his wife. She herself, however, has no such thought. Some.. thing like a' barrier has sprung up of late 'between her and Prince Sergius, and Irene is so unhappy that her intimates cannot fail to note the white cheeks, and the circles about her ~pretty eyes. If Prince Sergins perceives them, he makes no sign, but, when ever he meets Irene, is graVely and solemly atten- tive to her, following her about like a shadow; but all the. spontaneity that existed in the first days of their acquaintance seems to have faded away. But it is not wholly this that appals Irene, and makes her dread rather than look forward to this fête.. There has arrived in London from Paris a Madame de Coulon,a young widow of about thirty, and very beautiful. She is a Russian; mar- ried to a French Marcjuis, who has been dead about three years. At least; this is what the chatty journals and her acquaintances tell Irene, for she herself has not yet' seen Madp,ine de Coulon; she only knows', also horn the same sources, that Prinee Sergrus is devoted to this lady, that he has invited her over to play hostess for him at his fête, and that report, though it is unac- quainted with detail, says she is his ward. . The day of 'tile fete has arrived, and Irene, who has not met the Prince since the talk about Madame de Coulon hat reached her, is worked to such a pitch of excited jealousy that she is quite ill, audit almost becomes doubtful whether she will be able to go to this gathering of which fashionabe London never, Ceases to prattle. Lath-. Fedora administers calming draughts and keeps her quiet during the day in a, darkened room,but she caanot altogether ascribe reasons for her daugh- ter's State, though she guesses that Prince Serguis is the cause. Like a wise woman, however, she asks no questions ; only both she and Irene are resolved that unless the girl is abkohitely dying she will chew at the fête to-night. Lady Fedora hopes,' perhaps in more wake than one, for great results from that fête. Ferdinand,she is told, is to be' there—Ferdinand, who has not to her knowledge come • into - town from Hounslow since she heard of those bills which still dangled as a nightmare before her• and Henry Stan hope. • , It is only a week since she heard of them. During that week there has been a sort of lull, like the lull : that precedes a storm. Lady Fedora feels, but she does not know in what way, that Simon Knight's death in some manner affects the destinies Of her house. All this she would fain have cleared up, and she has a sort of idea that a crisis is at hand,and that at Prince Sergius's fête some of the thunder clouds will disperse. Not so Irene; she too expects a crisis, but with it she cantemplate.s a tcital collapse. The evening arrives—cloudless, starry, moonlit. Nature at all events it propitious. Irene with an effort gets up from the couch on which she has lain the whole afternoon, and is dressed in a toilette just arrived from Paris for the occasion. The suspenCe of the last few days has lent her beauty just - that touch of sorrow which spiritualises it, and both her father and, Geoffrey utter exclama- tions of 'astonished admiration when she joins them in the hall. Lady Fedora's exclamation is, however, the loudest when she aces Henry Stanhope, coat on arm, hat In hand. ' "You ! you are going with us to-night, Henry?" He nods his head and tries to smile. " The fête you kr ow is given by my old friend," he says ; "it would scarcely be courteous to stay away," So tuey all .f6nl get into the carriage, and throughout the whole drive,. ,even when they are dawdling along in what seems an almost intermin- able tail of carriages, not one Word is spoken by any Of them, so many and conflicting .are .the emotions witivwhich each mind is filled. Not even under the influence of the magical lights which shine above their heads as they slow,ly proceed along the avenue that leads to the villa,. nor the distant sounds of strange and unaccustomed music, are their tongues unloosed. At last they stand within the portals of the great Russian's fairy palace, arid he himself is on the 'threshold to receive them.

His reception 'of Henry Stanhope is moat cordial; he presents to Lady Fedora another Russian, of even higher rank than his own, whose arm she takes to mount the stairs, while Sergius places Irene's little trembling hand upon his own. " This-way, we pass through a drawing-room by a terrace walk to the gardens,' he he ,save softly, but sae searcely heeds his words; she is as it were bewitched by the scene, and faintness almost overcomes her. Gorgeous rare exotics fill the air with perfume; soft 'crimson shaded lights forbid all idea of glare ; sweet music, whose low warbling harmony is totally distinct from the weird sounds in the garden, seems to linger in the air as though played by spirit fingers ' • all -conduces to make Irene speech- less; she only feels that her band is ,on Sergins Lenekoffs arm, and that the magic -spell ef this man is around her, holding her with a resistless power. At the top of the staircase stands Berthe de Coulon. Irene's fingers tighten on Prince Sergius' arm -as she sees her, and the introductlon which conven- tionality demands is accomplished, Madame de Coulon holding out a tiny hand to Irene, and bid- ding her welcome. The society journals are right, the new comer. is beautiful ; but it is rather as the representative of night than day that Berthe de Coulon should be depicted. She is a brunette with ' keen, almost wicked eyes, that dance and sparkle, and are ever restless as though they could never see or know enough ; and she has a small, firmly-set mouth, denoting more power and self-will than seems wholly compatible with her'tiny frame. But it is only when her factgis in repose that this is notice- able ; when her lips, as they usually are, are wreathed into a' smile, the expression of her face is so bright, tile pearly row of teeth that; are revealed so dazzling, that even a hypercritical observer forgets sometimes, in the eootemplation of its rare and powerful beant?, all of which Madame de Conlon's face bids you beware. Irene was scarcely less struck by her than others had been, but she trembled and turned away from her; as though an asp had stung her. Why had Sergius Lenskoff brought this woman here? Was it as an insult or a warning, 'she wondered, and willingly would she have turned back and fled from that wonderful scene of beauteous delight which he had created • fled forth alone into the dark streets, if it might created; to die there. Ali ! had she only dared; but the hand that lay on Sergins Lenskoff's arm was tightened to his side. She could not draw it forth even had she decided to do so, and she was borne by him away from Berthe de Coulon's cruel eyes, away across thick piled Aubus- son carpets, and amid diamond Iledecked women and men resplendent in orders from every civilised land; away from this glittering crowd of bravery and beauty., on to the sileul terrace where the Moon shone in *old splendour above their heads, and the stars contended for the place of honour, with the myriads of coloured lamps which Aladdin himself seemed to have prepared for this fresh Arabian night of super- natural and mysterious beauty. Again the Weird lunge she had heard on entering fell on her ear, silencing as it did, the buzz of many voices • which .would otherwise have arisen from the gardens below. It was a lonely bend in the terrace to wide]] Prince Sergius had led her, where no gaping witne.ss could intrude on their privacy. "My beautiful loves are you satisfied? " hells*ked her ,in those rich ,low tones, which few- women could: withstand. "Is there anything in- all this scenethat does not please you?",. . Irene's answer was a sigh, while' soniething very much like a shiver passed over her, but she did not speak. "Whit is it—wkat has displeased you?" LIDA ihe looked up, into his, face she might hate notbd'such an amount of wrath gathered there as svon.ld, have made her quail, for Sergius-Lenskoff, accustomed to trample down every obstacle, °rooked no contradiction. Irene looked down rather than up, and whispered ray softly

have you bronght me here and shewn me ou ic this when ynow i weri., better I should go awal and never see your face again ?" "Wherefore ?" .he asked shortly, the gathering clouds on his brow well-nigh breaking into stairs; " Wherefore? who has bade you not to trust me ? "No one,'' she answered, clinging with her disen- gaged hand to the balustrade in front of her for the support she felt she needed in her single combat? with him. "No one could set me against you—flu" thing but my own woman's'instinet." "And it teaches you—?" Great heaven, if she had only noted then to the fullest the rushing of the mighty storm-tide those words conveyed what anguish and misery in the future might it have saved her; but in her tender heart she only thought sorrowing of the annoyance her mistrust was making for him after he had dou2 so much to render this fete a beauteous one, and still with averted eyes she answered, _ " It teaches me that I am not your only love, that there is no happiness for me in man's love t is to be shared by another." As-by magic the sun broke throngh the gathereo gloom upon magic brow. It was only jealousy aftel; all, where he had feared prejudice, and what man el Sergius Lenskolfs *type but delights in jealousy in. the' woman he loves? Her hand was rempved from his arm now, for the aim was round her 'waist, holding her as in a Yiee' , which rendered her well-nigh breathless: "My own, my only, my ,beautiful I" , She looked at him with her liquid eyes as thoua. astonished at his impassioned earnestness. Ile bent over her a,nd kissed the sweet upturned face. , "No one eau part, us, no voice, no evil tongue Say then, my own Irene, will you be my wife ?" ,he did not answer him for a moment, seareell. letting her head sink'upcin his .breast, and as thongll spell-bound by the magic scene and their own highlr wrought feelings, they stood for some seconds in g in speechless rapture. • Irene was the first to break the silence. Even

that blissful hour these was an intruding " gadame de Coulon ? " she asked, "will she ever come between us?" "Between us, my love ? You must be joking' there is- no one who can ever come between no'• Berthe de Conlon% love for me is not of the natnr you suppose." "Then she does love you?" asked Irene, raising her bead suddenly and trying to struggle Oval from him. . "As a daughter, aye—not with a lover's lova but do not let us talk of her, but of ourselves." Irene was not, however, so easily satisfied. , "Why, then, is she here?" was the next question. For a moment he would again have growl' angry; then the temper of his mind changed and /' smiled. , " Come with me," he said, . .
"let us return to

iestive throng from which, as host, I have perhaps right to be absent iso long, and you will yourself Ele: how events will shape themselves ; only promise ret before we go that whatever befall you will neve doubt my love for you." o "Never, unless I find you have deceived Me' .Ferdinand did not recognise her. "Perhaps you are already partly convinced% whispered the Prince. "We must not interrupt theril' let us do to others as we would be done by. " " But it is impossible. Ferdinand scarcely kno" this Madame de Coulon." . "Love's birth is instantaneous ,"he answered lauglY _ _ _ ,

ing, and by a tortuous path they returned one ino7 to the most crowded part of the gardens, where thei met Lady Fedora standing by her husband in the nact, unfashionable manner. She received Irene with 71 gentle reprimand for her long absence; if she 13/0 not been with the Prince there is little doubt bat would have been a far more severe one; Riit Lady Fedora was searetly,displeased, WI much not be said for Henry Stanhope. He had been sat, ing of late many things which he could in 7 prevent, but on love-makingbetween Sergins Lenslce4 and his sweet ,Irene he could never smile, could he bring himself to 'witness it withol she answered" and then woe is me for the unhaPP; ness I shall suffer." He gave her one more reassuring embrace and the4ll he led her by an' almost unobserved flight of Ater dawn on to the illurnimited and crowded gardens. Near a fountain round which seats had heed placed sat Berthe de Coulon playing with a fO,O golden tissue that shimthered as the light fell oil 10, Standing rather behind her was a man who was I:e3 ing over her talking with so much empresseal that he seemed to see no one else. Her last renlos4 evidently pleased him, and for a moment he thrsg his head up with a sort of triumphant toss. 40 lamp hanging just above him shone on his face' was Ferdnrand Stanhope. Irene gave a little surprised ery 'that made look round, but Prinee SergiuS led her down a Le 0 brilliantly-lighted path, and in the semi-de:loles making some effort to protest. irso "It makes us both, feel- very old, as we 100- 0 Irene and think of the merry past,when we.were 1300, youngsters together," he said, rather tartly, fullY.tely joying the way in which Prince Serguis Asia winced, though he essayed to observe, ples.ese , , that he did not feel old. 1. 0 "Still we have scarcely a couple of years 11 quarrel over," went on Henry Stanhope, purpeee , exasperating. a sn He was playing with edged tools, however, he speedily found out to his cost; for Sergli'u, Lenskoff was scarcely a Man to be trifled W,ll, especially when he had an important object in "You have grown old from care," he said ag,,s savagely; a man with a past like yours must beet 0 prematurely old. Efforts at hiding, my dear StanhoPto always fell, however sanguine you May be not te found out." "And have you n. ()thing to hide?" asked 0 Stanhope, trying to be off-hand, though his face 11- white as ashes. "Nothing that can in any way interfere wq4 - happiness," replied the Prince confidently. nemy Stanhope touched him on the arm tur him Just out of hearing of Lady Fedora and " Sergius," he said, "let the past be buried. Il.nil at the only man in Englandwho couldremind me of 0, dead." hot° "But in Petersburg there dwells a young , who trades extensivey With Paris in Russian furs- „1, "He knows nothing," was Henry Stanhope's ie most agonised whisper. "You alone can speak," merciful." "Then do not thwart mo in my strongdesire ; me Irene for my wife." (To be continual.)

THE GERMAN EMPEROR'SCONDITION.

On Saturday, the Emperor Frederick passed a mosft matisfactory day; he was able to walk about his rooms, ..end the fever has entirely abated. He was permitted LS , 'ex:ad the newspapers for the.first time for several weeks.'. careful examination of the throat by Sir Moron Mao. :krinzie shows that the local malady is making gradual. :Progress. Professor Visehow is to make a microscopical', 'examination of the expectoration. The Empress, onj -Saturday, visited the New Markets, accompanied by her daughter the Princess Victoria. The reception of that visitors was of a most cordial character. News of a favourable character continues from Berlin, "with respect to the condition of the Emperor Frederick,. .'erho is reported to be sleeping better, and suffering lerzi from the throat affection, Professor Virchow, after an Interview with the F.inperor yesterday, expremed him. 1 .self much puzzled with the case, and states that it is ' even now impossible to say whether the disease is can.. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

Acknowledging the receipt of a copy of a resolution __'lwasted by the Tottington Temperance Society, Mr: Isaac , says that he will vote against the compen- sation clauses. If the clauses are to be abandoned it can only be brought about by public meeting, as the majo- rity supporting the Government can only be turned from their purpose by public opinion. Mr. 11. Leake, ' oleo wrote to say he is opposed to the proposals. On Monday, the Executive of the Rossendale Unionist Association met at Rawtenstall. After the transaction of bnsiness relating to the organisation of the party, and ring aprangml for the annual meeting of the associa- Lim being held in June, a Conversation took plane upon' f'the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill, which Were condemned, and a resolution come to that a memo- rial against them be signed by Unionists and forwarded to Lord Harting,ton, requesting him to secure their with- drawal.

TUE COMPENSATION PROPOSALS. The Wesleyan Methodist Conference has forwarded the following resolution to the Government :—"That this Temperance Committee of the Wesleyan Methodist Conference respectfully and strongly urges the with- drawal of the compensation clauses of the Local Govern- Merit Bill on the following grounds :—(1) Because eqm- Pehsation is not required by law, precedent, or equity: (2) because the proposed transfer of revenue from houses licensed for the sale of intoxicating drinks to local bodies llootild create a corporate interest in the extension and perpetuation of the drink trade; and (3) because the local bodies would be elected on many other issues, and Would not, therefore, necessarily represent local option on the subject." The Rev. W. R. Shanks, of Newchurch, has laid a statement before Mr. Gladstone as to the opinion amongst Gladstoniqns, Liberal Unionists, &c., in the liossendale Division, with respect to the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill, adding that in his judg- ment it would greatly assist those who were working Altar the rejection of the clauses were he to give a definite statement of his views—(Ist) on the licensing clauses: 1211 d) on the principle of compensation. The following iraply has been received :—" May 11th, 1888, 16, James-, •Street, am desired by Mr. Gladstone-to , Acknowledge the receipt of your letter, and in reply to say that he is decidedly opposed to the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill, the provision for compen- aation, and all attempts to create a vested interest in the 'licensee taken out by publicans.—l am. sir, your obedient • servant, G. W. SPENCER LYITHLTON.—Rev. W.IL Shanks." The Matuthester brewers are not satisfied with the licensing proposals embodied in the Local Government t The Executive Committee of their Central Arsocia- Mon, as the result of recent conferences, have appointed eadeput, _ talon to seek an interview with Mr. Ritchie for 'the purpose of submitting, an alternative scheme, the blab of which is that license holders should be treated the same manner as when the power of granting -licenses was transferred from the Excise authorities ;to the magistrates, and that every licensee should be Acidified to a renewal of his license except on the Ulolloiting grounds :—First, that the applicant has failed :to produce satisfactory evidence of good character; I `lsecondly, that the premises, or any adjacent premises `dawned by the applicant, are the resort of disorderly per- sonas or used for immoral purposes; thirdly, that the MAPricant having previously held a license has forfeited The same through misconduct; and lastly, that he is not tip qualified by law. If their scheme were adopted, brewers say that there would be no necessity for "cermenstition, and the increased tax upon licenses Aught be withdrawn.

A conflict ensued near Denbigh, on Thursday, be- t Ween a ntimber of men who were distraining for tithe alul the onlookers. Upwards of thirty persons are said t4I have been injured. THE WARWICK BANK SCANDAL. At Warwick, on Thursday, Kelynge Greenway and George Green- tai, the principal partners in the bankrupt bank `„fr Greenway, Smith, and Greenway, were committed to take their trial upon various charges of having misap- ProPriated the Kingsley trust and falsification of the bank books. Kelynge Greenway was also committed or improperly dealing with the Cowper bill lodged with the bank for safe custody. Bail was fixed at £4,000 each for defendants and two sureties of £2,000 in each case. .igocriits - l SCHEME TO BRIDGE THE STRAITS OE DOVER.—The for News" Paris correspondent says :—A scheme r buildi— ng a bridge over the Straits or Dover has been °Plight out by the Creusot Company and M. Hersent, re well-known contractor. The bridge is to be about miles long, the superstiucture to rest 160 feet abovel,6oo the sea level, and the span between the piers to be feet. It is to bear four lines of rails, and each of Piers will contain a place of refuge and be surmoun.l by a powerful light. The estimated cost of the is £.32,000,000, and the construction will take .Ut six years. The scheme will shortly be laid before International technical committee, after which a r from the English and French Governments will applied for, no subvention being asked.

- The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS IN INOTA. The Marquis of RIPON asked whether the operation of the acts had been repealed, or only suspended, in India, and whether the allowances to women residing in regimental bazaars had been stormed.—Viscount Coss said the subject was first brought under his notice by the Bishop of Lichfield, and he at once placed himself in communi- cation with the Viceroy. The result was that what was known as regimental bazaars were stopped, and the operation of the Contagious Diseases Acts had been suppressed by the Government of India, Bombay, Mad- ras, and Basseni. With regal dto the circulars relating to allowances to women they had been withdrawn, and the allowances stopped.—The Marquis of Ilirox : Why not repeal the acts? They have been repealed in this cotmtry.—Viscount Guess said the Government of India only asked for the suspension, and the Govern- rolmtgave their consent to the council in order to see what the operation of their suspension would be. Surcmx OF A BRIDE.—A young woman, the bride of Joshua Strickland, farmer, Clitheroe, committed suicide at noon on Thursday in a most determined manner by hanging herself with a clothes-line. Her husband left her in the house at ten o'clock, and on returning to din- ner found the doors fastened. On getting through a window he found her dead in the cellar, banging to a hook. They were only married last Thursday. The affair is a mystery. OPENING OF THE ISLE OF MAN SEASON.—The Manx Line steather Queen Victoria, which left Liverpool 'at 11.10 on Thursday morning, reached Douglas at three o'clock, having accomplished the distanee in 3 hours and 50 minutes. She had on board about a thousand people, and arrived at Victoria Pier literally covered with flags. The pier was crowded with people, and the opening of the season by this line steamer was heralded with loud cheers.

Charles Cantor and George Anthony, who were charged on suspicion with being concerned in causing the death of Annie Smith, who was "found drowned in the river Lee, were-on Saturday discharged by the Dalston magis- trates for want of evidence.

From a uard and keys found in his pocket his name is believed to he G. A. Mellor, 108, Keswick-lane, Birmingham. The Home Secretary has decided to 'remit. eight years of the sentence of 20 years' penal servitude passed on young man named Prior, at' the iWinchester Assizes, in October last, for Bring a revolver at and wounding his sweetheart at Portsmouth. The memorial praying for mitigation of sentence had been signed by 10,000 persons.

- Twa Lerx PROFESSOR LEONE Luvr.—The remains of the late Professor Leone Levi were interred on Satztrday at the Highgate, Cemetery. There was a large crowd of people round the grave, and representatives came from nearly all the philanthropic and charitable institutions.:A wreath was sent from Mr. Charles Hancock on behalf the Paris Statistical Society. PRIZE Ficarr.—A prize fight took place on Sunday morning on the mountain between Merthyr and Aberdare., Both the combatants were Aberdare men. The arrange- ments had been very secretly conducted, and the affair was brought off without any interference on the part of the police. No fewer than.s-7 rounds were fought. Each • of the pugilists was severely punished, the elder especially being in a a most pitiful state.

ANOTHER ROMAN CATHOLIC PILGRIMAGE.—It is an- nounced that the Scottish Roman Catholics are organis- ing a pilgrimage ou a large scale to the island of lona, where Is situated the famous shrine of St. Columba. This saint carried Christianity from Ireland to Scotland, and founded a monastery, which is regarded as the cradle of Scottish Christianity. Many old Scottish kings are buried on lona. The pilgrimage is to take place on June 13th.

Speaking at his visitation at Leicester on Monday, .Bishop Magee said, however 'great and serious were the difficulties of the Church in large towns, he had no faith in or sympathy with the creation of a hybrid sort of clergy, half layman and half clergyman, with all the difficulties and disadvantages of both, and almost none of their advantages. What they required was efficient pastoral care, supplemented by faithful lay worker.'.

FUNERAL REFORM—The Duke of Westminster pre- sided, on Monday, at the tenth annual meeting of the Chiirch of England Burial, Funeral, and Mourning fleform Association, at Grosvenor House. Among those who took part in the proceedings were the Bishops of Gloucester and Bristol and the Lord Mayor of York. It was resolved to memorialise the Home Secretary to in- stitute an inquiry into the condition of town cemeteries ind the mode of burial with a view to legislation.

EXPLOSION : FIVR MEN Kizise.—Early on Monday morning an explosion, attended with fatal consegpences, occurred at the Aber Colliery, Tynewydd. On Sunday night, about eleven o'clock, seven men went into No. 3 level; and Bees Joseph, a man about 60, went somerdistance in to explore the workings. Two other men who should have awaited his return outside followed him, and shortly afterwards an explosion Occurred. Five men were killed, namely, Rees Joseph. married; Edward Gibbon, 24, single; Jenkin Stanford, 27, marred; Evan Jones, 18, single; and David Williams 30, single. It appears , that the fan employed for -vendlating the colliery had been stepped during Sunday, except for an hour pre- eeding the explosion. As soon as an entrance was pree. ticable the explorers went slown and recovered the bodies. .The old man Joseph had evidently crawled 1 about 80 yards after dropping his lamp, and his body was badly mutilated. The others showed less outward signs of injury. It was oTiginally arranged that the Royal party on their arrival should be received hy the Duke of Cambridge, but a note from the Duke's secretary was read at a withering of member* of the press apnouncitrg that, in ,coneequence of the Wolseley affair, the Commander-in-Chief' would have to ben his place in the afternoon in the House of Lords. Op their arrival the Prince and Princess were conducted to the dais. The National Anthem was then sung, and afterwards a Danish song by Mille. Bronnum, who was attired in Danish costume.

ALARNING FIRE ZS 14038R10R : BRAVE 11ESCUM—Great excitement was caused, ‘an early hour on Saturday morning, in St. Swithen's-lane and the vicinity of the Mansion flouse, London, by tho burning of the Bay Tree Tavern, owned by Mr. Gurney. No less than 16 persons, including the manager, his wife. and the barmaids who served on the premises, were asleep at the time of the outbreak. The unfortunate women appeared at the windows in their nightdressw, and in frantic tones appealed for help, as the flames were rapidly rising to the upper floors, notwithstanding the strenuous efforts of the firemen to subdue them. A fire escape being run up against the building, a number of firemen and policemen gallantly entered the room amid the flames, and rescued seven persons in a fainting condition, Sergeant Strong alone effecting the rescue of three. The remainder of the occupants were helped to escape on to the roof, and eventually reached places of safety. Fortunately, no one was seriously injured, and the fire was ultimately subdued,s=44=B. however, being done The rescue scenes by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress from-their draw. lug room window.

Drumard House, near Mohill, Leitrim, the residence or Mr. Wm. Jones, J.P., was burned to the ground on Monday night. 'Seven or eight farmers' houses were fired into by Moonlighters, at Knoclrnagree, near Castle Island, on 'Sunday night, but no person was injured. The accident to Mr. O'Brien, while driving with Mr. T. Harrington in a trap, was somewhat serious. His left hand will be practically useless for some time, and he is suffering severely from shock. . _ .

Mr. Se.xten LOrd Mayor of Dublin has received an address, signed ' •by Lord Aberdeen, Mts. Gladstone, and about 200 ladies and gent'amen, sympathising with the Irish party in their constitutional straggle. Mr. John Dillon, at Mell, Drogheda, on Saturday, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment, without hard labour, for inciting; the sentnnee to run concurrently with that passed on Friday. Notice of appeal was given. On Saturday afternoon, in the Dublin Law Courts, a jury found that the death of 38 hunters, the property of Captain Steeds, of co. Dublin, was caused bv malicious poisoning, and awarded Captain Steeds £3,000 damages. One juror disagreed, and held out for a long time, and complained of being bullied and threatened by his fel- low jurors. _ . .

A; an instance of the persecution to wlsich the nufor- tunate Mrs. Quirks, widow of the 'man who wee so brutally murdered nearTralee, fs subjected at present, is is worthy of note that a Mrs. Shea, who had the temerity to give a few nights' shelter to the widow, has just received a brutal threatening notice warning her that she will be killed if she again receives Mrs. Quirke into her house. THE LIBEL ACTION AGAINST THE TIMES. In the Queen's Bench, Dublin, yesterday, Mr. Ryan, Q.C., applied in the action of Prank Hugh O'Donnell, against the proprietor of The Times, for alleged libel, for an order of inspection under the Bankers' Act, of the accounts of the Land Lea Tue, the Ladies' Land League, and the 'National League with the Hibernian Bank, at the bank's Dublin offices, and their branch office at Tobercurry, co. Sligo. An order for the discovery had been made by the English Queen's Bench, but the bank officials denied the existence of accounts in the names mentioned. Counsel now relied on an affidavit that the moneys dealt with were the moneys of the association mentioned to the knowledge of the bank manager. The court refused the application in its present form. A subpcena was subsequently served upon Mr. Tenni- son Collins, secretary of the Hibernian Banking Company, to give evidence, and produce at the trial, at the next sitting in London, the hank books containing the accounts alleged to be from the Land League, the Ladies' Land League, and the Irish National League, "or by whatever. other names called."

div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

It is stated that Mr. Gladstone contemplates moving a vote of censure on the whole administration of the Crimes Act. The Liberal Council of the Buckrose Division of the West Riding have invited Mr. Angus Holden, of Bradford, to become the party candidate at the next election. At a meeting on Monday of the General Council of the Central Leeds , Liberal. Association it., was unanirnously resolved that Sir James Kitson should b. the Liberal can- didate for the division at the next election. Swakingat Liverpool on Sunday, Mr. Devitt said that .while the Isiah people were willing to take their religion and its interpretation from Rome, they would not sub- mit to political dictation from it. Ireland had done more for Catholicism in every quarter of the English- speaking globe than any other 'country, but if this was the gratitude that Rome was showing for all that Ireland had done for her, Irishmen might have to ask themselves some questions about it. • , • On Monday, the Hon. Geo. N. Curren, M.P. for the Southport Division, entertained a party of friends at dinner at the House of Commons, to meet the novelist, Mr. Rider Haggard. Mr. Gladstone dined with Mr. Murray, the eminent publisher, at his interesting house in Albemarle-street, which is replete with memorials of Lord Byron. Mr. Murray was present at the dinner in Edinburgh at which Sir Walter Scott avowed the author- ship of the Waverley Novels. His early love of travelling has left a permanent mark on the world in the shape of "Murray's Handbooks." The Marchioness of Salisbury on Tuseday unveiled, at the Mansion House, London, a portrait bust of the Prime Minister, which had been subscribed for by the Lord Mayor, sheriffs, alderriaen, and city councillors. The ceremony, which took place in the Egyptian Hall, was y e " company, including the rrtneeeir Ilutil a and, Lord Cranborne, the Lord' May ,o and city dignitaries. Srs,--For some weeks past I have been making some ,careful Investigations into the probable amounts which 'wottldbecorhe payable under the Comumasation Clauses ofMr.l3.itchit'sl3ill, in the event of its passing into law, and if the discretionary powers given to the new autho- rity were exercised. I enclose a few illustrations, selected from many hun- dreds upend iown the country, and shall be glad if you will publish them. In every instance I have had the property valued by some competent person in the neigh- bourhood, while the sales are in each Cs33o authentic. These casesare typical, and give a fair average of the whole.

I have not yet completed my investigation of the metropolis, but I am having a considerable number of houses, recently sold by auction, valued as ordinary business premises by one of the most experienced pro- fessional valuers in the city, and if you publish this communication, I will venture to trouble you presently with another about London public-houses. From the evidencel have been able to collect so far, I have no hesitation in placing the amount with which the Govern- ment propose to endow the liquor trade at from £200,000.000 to £250,000,000, the mist bulk of which will go into the pockets. of monopolist brewers and dis- tillers, and not into those of the tenants of public-houses. —Yours faithfully, W. S. CAINE. House of Commons, May Nth, 1888.

Sir Thomas Grove, the sitting member for the Wilton division of Wiltshire, severed his connection with the Liberal Unionists on being informed- that the Liberal Association had passed a resolution hostile to him. WHISKY IN 110SPITALS.—Much of the whisky supplied in workhouse and other hospitals is very new, and is often largely composed of "patent still whisky or silent spirit." We perceive that Messrs. W. &A. Gilbey have entered into an arrangement with Mr. John Jameson, the most famous of the Dublin distillers, by which they will in future supply the well-known JJ whisky, six years old at least, in sealed bottles with labels guaranteeing quality. It would be well if such whisky as this, the quality of which is absolutely guaranteed, were supplied to public institutions instead of the uncertain stuff so often administered to the sick. We understand that the above whisky is bottled under the supervision of Her Majesty's Excise officers, which offers a perfect guarantee that it is John Jameson's We manufacture.—Medical Press and Circular, May 9th, 1888.
