Mr. Thomas Cooper Turner, of Eastcheap, London' wholesale sugar dealer, fired a revolver bullet through his head on Thursday morning on Putney Hea,tit. He was still alive in the afternoon. o TERRIBLE LEAP.—On Thursday morning, a patient at the Sheffield Infirmary, named Thomas Crossland, jumped from one of the windows of that institution, a height of 60 feet. He was not delirious but wanted to go home, permission to do which was refused until the doctor had seen him. A couple of nurses saw him get through the window and they clung to his clothing, but he wrenched himself from their grasp. Be is seri- ously injured. MR. BALFOUR AT BATTERSEA. MT. A. J. Bal- four, M.P., speaking on Wednesday night at Battersea to the members of the local -Conservative Association, replied to Mr. Gladstone's recent statements at the gathering of Nonconformist ministers. One of the most notable of Mr. Gladstone's fictions, he said, was that the Crimes Act had been used, not against crime, but against combination. What foundation was there for that charge? The only two combinations attacked were boycotting and the Plan of Campaign, and was the right lion, gentleman prepared to say that neither of these conspiracies ought to be assailed? Then he asserted that during Mr. Gladstone's term of office cumulative sentences had been passed, and said it was painful and disgusting to find men of the position of Mr. Gladstone and Sir George Trevelyan sheltering themselves in this way behind their bad memories. Mr. Balfour went on at great length in a similar strain, and said at the pre- sent moment the Government were fighting the cause of law and freedom in Ireland, and he had yet to learn that that was not the came of true religion, ror all kinds ef doinestte eearuag, Bagley and 'Wright a cotton is the beat.—Adot.

Lost, wiThsELEy has had, as the phrase goes, to climb down " witb aeference to his tall state- with regard to 'he low and vicious stan- Lard of morality" possessed by the ministers who '4l4re from time to time the gontrol of the army ci navy, In the same speech be also said the .4.8 t thing one sees when a naw Administration i,eencles into power is "an endeavour awl!) by the inister in office to obtain some clap-trap reputa- -41'1°4 by cutting down the expense of the army and It was impossible for the present Govern, tient to let such statements pass and still retain ' their self-respect ; and we are not at all sur- Zlled at the vigorous attack which the PRIME vetNnsun made upon Lord WOLSELEY in dealing tloth the subject, on Friday week, in the House of 1.4. "Our only General" replied to Lord l'lsircrav in his place in the House of Lords on ~9ndav • and he stuck pretty well to his iii asserting that our Army aria Navy Paratively weak. But he was very careful to 'lce it clear that when he spoke of the "low ,411,,t1 vicious standard of morality" which pre- in the Ministry he had no particular 1847 in his mind. With regard to this phase the controversy, Lord GRANVILLE humorously 11711arked that, while the Ansrurwrr-GENERAL had ye the most ample apology to the noble Mar- 'who attacked him, he had made no apology iv tile members of the late Government who had 't him alone. But Lord GRANVILLE might have p.fs,:itle further ; he might have reminded Lord tqalar.rr that when Mr. GLADSTONE was in office L,1886, and when there was some danger of war tn..°3•king out with Russia, there was a supple- t;:itavY vote of no lees than Eleven Millions to '"wle such men as the Ansruvarr-GENERAL to t the A.rmy and Navy in good fighting order. tllalanily for both countries, war was averted; b anka to the tact and firmness of Mr. GLADSTONE, lit Most of the money was spent for all that; and /vhat the nation has a right to ask in view of the 154Nent scare is—what was done with it—how was it T't? It is all very well for Lord WOLSELEY to ;,,g: that the mistake which the authorities make il,at they never take the people into their confi- katie% If he means by this, as we take him to 81104'1, that, if the people only knew all, they would elia../4r more millions upon the officials who have thTe of military matters, we venture to say 4.,.they would do nothing of the kind. It th "'Mays the cry of military men that e service is going to the dogs. They are ilellastingly asking for more money. They are e the daughters of the horse-leech, whose con- cry is "give, give !" Our army is, man for arl, the most costly army in Europe. In 1881 :cllBB2, as Lord SALISBURY pointedly remarked, 4e Were spending a little over Two Millions h Year in new war ships and armament for ships; tLit for the last two years the expenditure under at head has been more than double that sum; thhas been over Five Millions a year. In 1880 t: total cost of the army and navy was I:5)250,000, last year it was 31,690,000. " our army is not what it should be, it is not be- Zell% sufficient money isnot spent upon it; itisnot ).• 4118 n the soldier, who is furnished with dry bread, tt-' too well fed; it is because there are too many hlißtocratic parasites professing to act as officers, vilt in reality meddling and muddling and wasting I)" substance of the people. We foresee as the ollteome of all this talk about the weakness of our hefooces a further demand upon the patience and 'tellree of the taxpayer; but if we could have our haY the answer would be that patience is ex- iziansted, and the purse is closed. Thirty Millions Vast sum to contribute year by year for the „.4r4lY and navy. Whatever Lord WOLSELEY may t'4Y, it ought to ensure us against the possibility all enemy marching on and taking possession of i"ldon. If it does not, there is bungling, or ex- ivegance, or maladministration somewhere, and time to make an example of an Adjutant- "elleral or a Commander-in-Chief. Englishmen not to be frightened into attempting to raise 444e1l monster armies as are undermining the real ' l'ength of our Continental neighbours. We are k*cled by the sea, and that to us is worth a intUilion of armed men. Let us by all means see to ththat our army and navy are efficient; but for taZt purpose what is needed is that economy shall t e the place of extravagance—energetic action :4lte place of the paralysis of red tape. The ‘'etitial need is not more "brass," but more brains.

4:43s National Radical Union, of which Mr. 1.1 CHAMBERLAIN is president, does not appear 13sk• able to do anything" national" or "radical" (.1 ; and so it was called together, on Satur- -1141_3' night, to assist in bringing into the world is to be known as the Rural Labourers' agos.• There was a time when Mr. JESSE t;')/4-INos was chairman of the Allotments Associa- -441; but the members of that body thought fit to 4tlll'oint another chairman, an act, Mr. Cif.tivinEn- t..AlN flays, of "ingratitude, and folly, and bad t7te." The Allotments Association existed, in the of the Chamberlain family group, in order tatll. COLLLNGS might have a chairmanship; tild so, on his heing deposed, the Rural Labourers' :ague is started in order that he may still have ething to preside over. It was fitting, the h• niberlainites will think, that the new league k'ould • - be inaugurated as something subsidiary to National Radical Union; for it would never ev b for en Mr. COLLINS to shine, except with ilo°,l*.r°lvecl light from the Chamberlain sun. It is of `,vorthy, however, that Mr. COLLINGS is spoken bY Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as having by his exertions

swelled the Liberal majority in 1885,1' to a greater extent than by those of any other leader, however distinguished." This, of course, means that Mr. GLADSTONE was as nowhere in the struggle com- pared with Mr. JESSE Comaxas ! How considerate of the member for West Birmingham to make this known for the benefit of the future historian; the world would otherwise have been oblivious of the remarkable fact. But if Mr. COLLINGS is thus able to surpass "any other leader, however distin- guished," it follows that even the great Mr. CHAMBERLAIN must be small beside him; and, that being the case, ought not" our Jesse" be president of the National Radical Union, while Brother Joseph goes down a step to his right place as chair- man of the smaller league ? s Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is as modest as he is great, it is merely necessary to call his attention to the incovgruity of the pre- sent state of things in order to have it rectified. Perhaps, too, whilst he is in the way of making crooked things straight, he will explain how it is that nothing has come of the Allotments Act passed by the Unionist Government of which ho is so enamoured. Ihe labourers who have mastered its provisions say it is a delusion and a snare, and that it was never intended to be of any benefit to them. To ordinary minds, it would seem that the workman who could set all the:machinery of the law in motion which would be requisite before he could compel a landowner to grant him the use of .au. acre of land, would he qualified for taking chatge of the woolsack rather than a cowshed. It would be interesting, too, to know what Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is driving at when he speaks of the "factious party that take their policy as they take their pay from the enemies of this country ;" and whether he regarded himself as an enemy of his country when he suggested that MT. PARNELL, as the leader of the "factious party," should be made Chief Secretary for Ireland? The member for West Birmingham ought to remember that he has still a few followers left, and that they are entitled to pf,wiodic explanations, so that they may know where siopt and what lie is about. It would be un- fortunate if the impression should get abroad that the coat of nueiy colours which Joseph wears was related in some way Cc, the many colours of the partig.§ with which he has been many Leagues ai:tl associated in his extraordinary career.

ITHE Local Government Bill, there is every reason to believe, will be considerably altered and imprj7ed hefore it passes into law. Strong efforts are being made with a view to convert all towns with a population of about 50,000 into counties under the Bill. It is with the object of showing that Warrington Itas a good claim in this respect that a poll has just been taken of the number of inhabitants. The total popu- lation does not yet reach the 60,000, but it is so near that number, and the growth of , the borough is so steady, that it is hardly I likely to be left out in the cold. There is this, too, to be said, that its situation on the border- land of Lancashire and Cheshire especially lands itself to the creation of a town-county without interfering with adjoining areas. St. Ilelens, with a population of 60,000,ha5,0f course, a special title to consideration, and so, too, has Wigan. There is ample reason as the bill stands for munici- palities desiring to become self-contained counties; for, apart from the obvious fact that it means an extension of the principle of local self-government, it means, too, a reduction of county taxation. Assuming that Liverpool, Manchester, Blackburn, and half a dozen other places in Lancashire be- come counties in themselves, and thus cease to contribute to Lancaster as a county, it is clear that the burden will fall all the heavier on those that remain in the original county. This is one of the difficulties of the bill, and one, too, of its many glaring defects. The fact is the bill violates so many of the principles upon which it is assumed to be based that it is inequitable in several respects— apart from the fraudulent proposals to endow brewers and publicans. It is revolutionary in some of its provisions, and the worst of it is that those who have drafted the provisions do not seem to have any clear idea of what will be their effect when brought into operation. It would be well, therefore, if the bill could be knocked on the head during the present session, and licked into some- thing like shape next year.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The unmarried ladies of Halton have been hav- ing what was called a Spinsters' Tea Party. They did not exclude gentlemen or married ladies—by no means • but it was provided that gentlemen or married ladies should be fined if they gave assis- tance in any form. Just so; this is leap year; let the spinsters have a fair chance of showing off their good points. Something may come of it.

At Haydock, they have this week provided the fifth annual treat to old people over 60 years of age. This mode of making the old folks happy is a rowing institution; and it is to be hoped it will spread throughout the country. There is no danger of imposition in dealing with old and well- known people. The poor we have always with us, and it is true charity to brighten the lives of the deserving poor.

The "World," referring to the visit to Black- burn of the Prince of Wales, says :—" At the ban- quet the Mayor commenced his speech with the words Your Worship, ladies, and gentlemen,' which he afterwards vainly endeavoured to cor- rect." Is it not more likely that Mayor Appleby really said "Your Warghip," having regard to the Prince as the greatest "gun" he had ever enter- tained. H.R.H. was entertained; he says so.

A Widnes man and three others were ordered, at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, to receive twenty lashes with the "cat," for robberies accom- panied with violence. It is satisfactory to learn from Mr. Justice Day that the " cat" is effective as a deterrent to this particular class of crime. Offenders who have once felt the lash avoid the risk of such punishment for the future. The basks of these brutes in human form are sensitive if their consciences are seared.

It seems that the London City Board of Guardians have been obtaining boys' and girls' boots, under a contract, at sixpence per pair! This is surely sweating the life out of the boots and the bootinakers. Oddly enough, it transpired that as much as is. Bd. per pair had heen paid the contractor for repairs of the same class of boots. But even then 2s. 2d. per pair is not much for new boots and repairs. Perhaps Mr. Haynes, who is great on boots, will explain the mystery.

It is to be hoped the Government will stick to the King-Harman Salary Bill. It is hanging like a rope round their neck; and they were pretty nearly throttled with it in the House of Commons, on Monday evening. Mr. Heneage is a Liberal Unionist, but he will have none of it. He moved an amendment to strike out the proposed Salary; and on a division the Government had a majority of eight only. But the Tories will persevere, for they are the stupid party. And whom the gods would destroy they first make mad. A Liverpool contemporary states that Millais's picture of Mr. Gladstone, which was once owned by the Duke of Westminster, and the • disposal of which formed such an interesting incident in the Northwich election, is now the property of Lord
Rosebery, and is going to Melbourne for the Oen. tennial Exhibition.

The Duke of Westminster is ruining his reputaL tion by his blind political partisanship. It ap- pears, writes a London cOrrespondent, that Mr. Robert Spencer, M.P. for Northamptonshire, Lord Spencer's half-brother and heir presumptive, and Mrs. Spencer, were engaged to dine with the Duke at Grosvenor House on Friday night. On the day following the Eighty Club dinner to Mr. Parnell, Mr. Spencer received a letter from the Duke say- ing that, as he had observed Mr. Spencer's name among the guests who met Mr. Parnell, he must re- quest him to consider the invitation to Grosvenor House withdrawn. The Duke has a right, of course, to "play the fool in his own house ; " but this would be called boycotting if it were done in Ire- land.

The Liberal Unionists made a good deal of the reception, in Dublin, which was given to Lard Har- tington and Mr. Goschen when they went there to beat the big drum. "The cause "—whatexer that may mean—was progressing; aud there was con- , fidettee, amongst some of them, that they could win the bye-election which took place last week. But, alas ! for their hopes. When the result of the poll was declared, on Saturday, it was founel that Mr. T. A. Dickson, the Home Rule can- didate, had been returned by a majority of 1887. And now the Liberal Unionists speak of the elec- tion with tsys in their voices.

Chatwood4 " the safe man," is 146 t afraid of Mr. Fletcher's 'blowpipe and compressed 6xygen— that is if his best steel safes, two inches thick, are to be put to the test, It seems to be admitted that, with the use of the blowpipe, it would be pos- sible for the scientific burglar to make his way into an, ordinary safe. Airid this is Mr. Fletcher's point. It comes to this with the average trades- man, that his safe is not gate, after all. But the average tradesman keeps a burFking account, and does not have much money about for the enter- pnsing burglar to lay hands on.

The officials and parishioners of the Warrington Parish Church have been over-ridden in the matter of yielding up a slice of their district for the enlargement of St. Peter's district. Jut t now they are realising what is the meaning of the connection between Church and State. It is the Privy Council that has finally stepped in and settled the matter. We are not expressing any ' opinion as to the wisdom of the decision, but ven- ture to remark that if the parishioners of St. Zlphin's desire to have a voice in their own affairs, they 040401449 qt? must hall) in the flu-gement for dis-

At the suggestion of the Solicitor to the Trea- sury, the editor and the printer of the " St. Helens Lantern" have been prosecuted by the Chief Con- stable of St. Helens for a breach of the Lotteries Acts. How is it that no prosecution has followed upon the gross breach of the law at Warrington to which we referred the other week? Is there one law for St. Helens and another for Warring- ton? Or is the " Observer "to be allowed to do I wrong with impunity because it is a Tory paper? It looks bad—this winking at one editor as a "rogue and vagabond," and hauling the other before the magiatrates,

Tven the brewers are beginning to realise that there is no chance of perpetrating such a fraud upon the public as the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill. The Manchester Brewers Association therefore propose to forego any claim for compensation, if they can, practically speak- mg, be guaranteed the possession of the licences they at present hold. But John Bull will surely not be such a fool as to tie his hands in this way. It is admitted by all sections of politicians that there are too many drink-shops; and, this being so, it is the plain duty of the Legislature, and of the community, to set about reducing the number.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1888.

POOR RATE FOR HALTON.—The Runcorn magistrates have sanctioned the laying of a poor rate of Is 241 in the £ for the township of Halton. Witorns FREE LIBRARY. -- During the month ended May 10th, the attendance of persons at the Widnes Read- ing Room was 12,135, averaging 504 daily. The books borrowed during the same period was 4.949, a daily average of 206. • NARROW ESCAPE FROM POISONING AT WIDNES.—A young girl, daughter of Mrs. Ashley, 41, James-street, Widnes, swallowed a packet of vermin powder, in mis- take for teething powder, and immediately showed 'alarming symptoms of poisoning. An emetic was given by Dr. Hutchinson, and the child is now progressing favourably. MILL Buow WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOLS, RUNCORN.— The anniversary of this school was celebrated on Sun- day, when the Rev. J. Bateman, of Burton, fgrinerly of the Runcorn dr ; preached two sermons, in Halton- road chapel. There was a good congregation at both morning and evening service. The choir, assisted by the scholars, rendered specially selected music. The collections in aid of the school amounted to £2l I.Os Od. RUNCORN STARR BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—In connection with the first Runcorn Society an appropria- tion took place iu M.r. W. Handley's office on Monday evening. Mr. Povah presided. Messrs. Collings and Kniveton were appointed scrutineers, and Master Faulk- ner was appointed balloter. The result of the ballot was that Mr. John Garner, joiner, of Frodsham' becomes en- titled to a loan of £2OO for 12i years free of interest. Mn. JACK pRIGGS IN AUSTRALIA.—MT. Jack Briggs, the Lancashire county, professional, has just returned , from Australia, where he has been a member of Shaw and Shrewsbury's cricket team. It will be interesting to our Widnes readers to learn that " Jack " has made a capital record. In the batting averages he appears 4th on the list, following Shrewairy, Ulyett. and M. Read. He played in 38 matches, was four times not out, and scored a total runs of 705, giving an average of 20.26 per innings. The highest score he made in an innings was 80. In the bowling averages he also occupies a promi- nent place. He bowled 4,787 balls sending up 622 maidens, and he obtained 208 wickets at a cost of 6.105 runs per wicket. The total ruin made from his bowling was 1,353.

ACCILENT TO THE WIDNES CRICEETCLUBPROFESSIOWA.L. —Mr. James Briggs, professional to the Widnes Cricket Club, met with a singular accident on Saturday after- noon. The eleven had'played a match with St. Helens Recreation, on the ground of the latter, and were on their way to the station to return home, when Mr. Briggs got one of the long bags he was carrying en- tangled in his legs. He was thrown violently forward, and alighted on his head. He was picked up in an un- conscious state and conveyed home' where Dr. Nealon was called in, but he remained in that state until Mon- day morning. Afterwards he recovered rapidly, and is now able to leave the house. He is, however, not in a fit condition to play, and his son Jack, who has just retnrned from Australia, will take his place in the team. PRIiitTLVE METHODIST CH&PEL, RUNCORN.—The anni- versary services were held in this chapel, Greenway-rd., on Sunday last. The pulpit was occupied in the morn- ing and evening by the Bev. T. Law, f Millom, Cum- berland, and in the afternoon the Rev. E. Hall, of the Methodist Free Church, Runcorn, Was the preacher. There was a large congregation at eae.h service and col- lections were made in aid of the school funds. In con- nection with the anniversary a miscellaneous entertain- ment was given in Regent-st. Sunday school on Monday evening. The "Friends of Temperance," a number of young men from Widnes, provided the programme, and catered for the enjoyment of those present in a manner which reflected the greatest credit upon them. Anthems, duets, readings, and recitations were capitally rendered, land the services of the 'friends were suitably acknow- I ledod. The chair wag Occupied by Mr. John Wilsonrthe architect and surveyor. The total amount realised in aid of the Sunday schools was £25 7s. WIDNES DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—Last evening week, the annual meeting for the election of the repre- sentatives upon the District and Executive Councils of the Widnes Division Liberal Association was held at the Reading-room, Garston, under the presidency of Mr. Bowrine. There was a good attendance, about 400 members being present. In the course of a short address the Chairman spoke of the work done by the association during the past year. He alluded to the fact that they had held sixteen public meetings within the division during that period, and otherwise done a great deal of good work. Net Withstanding the loss of some of their Tatlontrit frtends, the htimber of their subscribers had increased to nearly 400; and their financial position although not all that could be desired, was much better than it had been. The District and Executive Councils were then elected, and the proceedings terminated with a lecture on "Ireland," by Mr. W. H. Handley, of Run- corn, which he accompanied by limelight illustrations.

MRS. AND MISS BRDNNER AT TIN DRAWING-ROOM.—At the Drawing-room, held on Wednesday, by command of the Queen, at Buckingham Palace, by the Princess of Wales, Mrs. J. T. Brunner was presented by Mrs. Glad- stone. She wore a cream satin skirt draped with China crepe, caught up with cream feathers; panels of Indian embroidery. The corsage and train were of a golden- brown velvet, the latter lined with cream satin and trim- med down one side with Indian embroidery and with two plumes of feathers on the other side. The corsage was trimmed with lace and feathers. Mrs. Brunner wore as ornaments, diamonds and Indian jewellery, and on her head she had cream feathers and tulle veil. She carried a bouquet of Marechal Neil roses, and golden-brown orchids of the same shade as the velvet. Miss Brunner was presented at the Drawing-room by her mother. She wore a white tulle dress, looped up tivith lilies of- the valley, train and corsage of white Bengaline silk, trim- med with the same flowers, ornaments, and pearls. Miss ISrunner carried a posy of lilies of the valley and maiden- hair [Ms. A Vtoti.tr NAVVY AT RUNGORN.—Before Major Hazle- hurst, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Geo. Beres- ford, a navvy, was charged with begging. Torn Clough, butcher, Regent-st., said about half-past seven on the previous evening the prisoner entered his shop and asked for help, stating that he had only had one cup of tea since morning. He refused to do so, and the prisoner "looked him in the face for about three minutes," and had his fist raised in a threatening attitude. The prisoner said" I have seen you before, and I will see you again; I have you dotted." He (witness) was so upset that he could not remember the whole of what took place.—P.C. Ratcliffe said the prisoner was drunk.—Superintendent ' , Hollingsworth informed his worship that the prisoner was a most violent man. When placed in the cell he threa- tened tir kill himself, and he attempted to break his skull by running with his head against che wall. He was therefore strippEd of his clothing, and put in a cell where he could not do any damage.: A constable also watched him throughout the night. The prisoner said he had got work on the Ship Canal, and he earnestly pleaded to be discharged.—He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. Biviw A MAN'S HAND AT WIDNES.—At Liverpool As,. sizes on Monday, Catherine Lawrenson, aged 34 years, of no occupation, pleaded not guilty to maliciously wounding George Jackson with intent to do him griev- ous bodily harm, at Widnes, on April 14. Mr. Swift prosecuted. The prosecutor is a, labourer living at Wid, nes, and about five o'clock on the afternoon of April 14 he went with a friend into the Central Hotel, Widnes, to get a glass of beer. The prisoner was there, and as soon as she saw him she used a foul expression, and said ' "That's him who gave lily man fourteen days." It seemed that a month ago Jackson had occasion to bring. the prisoner's friend up before the magistrate. Finding she was inclined to be violent he went out of the public. house, but she followed him, and, after using threaten- ing language, struck him on the face. Another man knocked him down, and the prisoner then kicked him on the cheek. When Jackson got lap he put out his left hand to protect his face, upon which the prisoner bit his little finger. She got his hand in her mouth a second time, and again bit the same finger. Four wounds were caused to the finger, and the result was that blood poisoning supervened, extending up the arm. For some time there was danger that the arm must be amputated. The prosecutor stated that he gave the pri- soner no provocation.' The jury found the prisoner guilty. There were many convictions recorded against her. His lordship sentenced her to nine month's impri- sonment with hard labour. •

-- SPINSTER TEA PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT AT HAL- TON.—A somewhat unique tea party hnd entertainment were held at Halton, on Friday evening, at the Parish Church Schools, in aid of the Church Improvement Fund. It was entirely arranged by the unmarried ladies of Hal- ton, assisted by a few of their Runcorn sisters, and styled "The Spinsters' Tea Party." It proved a com- plete success, both socially and financially. At each tray there WAS a waitress and a fine-taker, and all the spin- sters who took teat were distinguiihed by a spray of ivy , and white dahlias, which they wore. A fine of one penny was demanded of all gentlemen and married ladies who helped or gave assistance in any form, and great amusement was caused during the evening by the vigil- ance of the fine-takers, few of the visitors escaping at , least the payment of one fine. At the entertainment which followed glees were ably rendered, Miss Wright being pianist. Miss Clara Taylor gave "I dreamt I dwelt" in a most charming style. Miss L. Worthington contributed pianoforte solo, and Miss Wright sang"A Country Lass" in a tasteful manner, and for an encore "Three Wise Men." Mddle. Notsnhoj delivered a modern sermon. Miss L. Wood sang "Flow far is it called to the grave ? " and "Aunt Tabitha" very effectively. The Misses Taylor and Wright contributed a duet, which was enthusiastically received, whilst Miss Pierpoint ren- dered "Darby and Joan" in a most pathetic manner; :and Miss Short gave an admirable reading of "The Well of St. Keyne." A representation of Mrs. Jarley's Wax- works met with cordial reception, and was admirably carried out. Miss Johnson took the part of Mrs. Jarley, and Miss Lilian Ayers made a very nice and effective "Little Nell." The "Gypsy Operetta" was also a great success, in which the following took part :—Misses E. Watkin, A. Acton, D. Chadwick, H. Acton, A. Jea cock, E. Lambert. Haddock, Potter, C. Lambert, Wilkinson, J. Lambert, M. Bradburn, A. Potter, B. Potter, and L. Wright. Miss Amy Johnston was the accompanist. Miss Worthington, as chairwoman, was eberything that could be desired. The fund realised amounted to £l3 5s 6d, including a few subscriptions. Great praise is due to Miss Short for the indefatigable energy she displayed in getting up the affair, and the success she attained.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

11...* A REPLY AND A CHALLENGE.—OD Saturday, April 14th the Warrington Guardian said as to its circulation that it was "many times greater than that of all our local contemporaries combined." As we have good reason to doubt so extraordinary 'a statement, we are willing to put this trumpet- blowing to a practical test. We, therefore, offer ,1 to submit our books to any firm of accountants 11 agreed upon, on the understanding that the pro- prietors of the Warringto4 Gitardian do the same ; and we undertarco to subscribe £lO to the War- ri ton Infirmary if, as the result of the investiga- tion, it is not shown that the Warrington and Mid- Cheshire Examiner has a LARGER SALE in the borough of Warrington than our boastful contem- porary. We mention the borough of Warrington because it is a distinct and definite area, the cen- tre of local population, and the head quarters of both newspapers. The further condition stipula- ted is that the proprietors of the Warrington Gitcrelian shall engage to subscribe £lO to the Infirmary if they, on their side, fail to make good a similar claim. By SALE, we mean the total number of papers for which payment can be shown to have been received; the time covered to be the first three months of the present year. As the Warrington Guardian is a bi-weekly journal, either the Wednesday's or the Saturday's issue can be taken for comparison. It is time the public ascertained, beyond cavil, what there is behind this bounce on the part of our local con- temporary, and whether it will be able to boast when it has been brought to book. We have only ! to add that this challenge will be open for ac- ceptance for four weeks from the date of its issue (April 21). -

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances, when they first find their eyesight failing, they purchase all kinds of in- ferior manufactured spectacles, which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, and 44, Market-st., Manchester, 143, Lord-st., Southport, and GO, Whitefriargate, Hull, has invented his "Per- fection" Spectacles, which ha adapts at either of the above addresses at 7s (id per pair. He will guarautee that they are not to be equalled in the coun- try for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "how to preserve the sight " free on application.—Advt. A WRECK IN THE MERSEY AT RUNCORN.-b—LaSt week 1 end the barquentine Dunleary, whilst being towed down the river by a Weston Point steam packet, grounded upon a sandbank opposite Ince, and the tug was com- pelled to leave her. At the next flood tide efforts were , made to get the vessel afloat, but without avail, and she has worked herself into the bed of the river in such a fashion that ou Wednesday it was clear that the Dun- leary would have to be destroyed, as there was no hope of saving her. The vessel, which belonged to Dublin, was carrying a cargo of 400 tons of rock salt for Mr. H. A. Falk, of Winsford, to Newcastle-on-Tyne. The cargo , was not insured. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMaITPCEE.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday evening in the Town Hall. Mr. F. A. Lake presided, and there were present: Messrs. J. Simpson, F. J. Norman, T. Riley, and J. D. Jones (librarian.) The librarian reported that during April there were 1,975 volumes issued from the lending library and the reference department, classified as fol- lows :—theology, 36, philosiphy, 6, science and-art, 44, history, 172, poetry,l9, fiction, 1,544, miscellaneous, 154. The receipts amounted to £2 Os 7d. Several volumes had been presented during the month. It was resolved that the library should be closed on Whit Tuesday. This day is observed as a holiday in the town, and last year the applications to borrow books were extremely few in number. The news room will be open as usual. A NEW LocomonyE AT WlDNES.—Messrs. Hall Bros. and Shaw, chemical manufacturers, Widnes, have just introduced into their works a new and powerful locomo- tive. The engine is of a most handsome design, and is well adapted for the work it will have to perform. Weighing 24 tons, it has cylinders 14 inches in diameter with a stroke of 20 inches. The wheels have a diameter of 3 feet 2 inches, and are fixed to run upon railway metals with a guage ot 4 feet 81 inches. The capacity of the water tank is 660 gallons. The engine has been supplied by the well-known firm of Beckett and Sons. of Bristol, who have manufactured engines for the Ship Canal works, arid also for several works in Widnes. The christening of the engine was made the occasion of an interesting ceremony. At the invitation of Mr. Shaw, a party of ladies and gentlemen assembled in the works to take part in the function. Miss Ella Shaw mounted the , iron monster, and set it in motion, at the same time con- ferring her own name of " Ella " upon it.

THEFT OF A VALUABLE DOG AT RUNCORN-. William Millington, alias "Pheasant," a boatman was brought before Mr. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, charged with having on the 12th.in.st., at Weston Point, stolen a dog, value £5, the property of Edward Evans, employed at the salt works. The prisoner was remanded. PA.RNWORTH AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—This society appears to have ended its care:ir. A meeting of the cmamittee was recently summoned, but only Mr. Win. Longton and four other members attended. A statement of accounts showed that the society was still £2O iii debt to Parr's Banking Company, and it was resolved to ask the Bank to remit the same, as it was impossible to raise the money. Another meeting is to be held shortly for the purpose of considering whether a show shall be held again. ThE UNITED TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION, WIDNEE.-The , delegates of the various local temperance societies have held a meeting for the purpose of arranging for again holding a I united temperance demonstration on some day during, this summer. It was resolved that a demonstration should be held, and that a guarantee fund of 10s per society should be formed. Nearly the whole of the socie- ties have signified their willingness to aid in the under- taking. The following officers are appointed :—Chair- man. Mr. S. Lamb; general secretary, Mr. W. Rigby; corresponding secretary, Mr. J. Thompson; treasurer, Mr. W. Wilcock. PETTY PILFERERS sr RUNCORN.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Monday, George Hope, a boatman from Winsford, pleaded guilty to having that morning slept in the works of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company at Weston Point.—The prisoner said he was on his way to Manchester looking for work, and he stopped at Weston Point to rest.—Superintendent Hollingworth said it was only by keeping away from the town these tramps and vagrants that a stop could be put to the petty thefts that occurred. These men had a remarkable aptitude for taking anything that was loose.—The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. CRUELTY TO A RUNCORN BUTCHER'S PONY.7-At Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. John Brun- drit and Mr. G. L. Davies, George Booth, butcher, Regent-st., was charged with cruelly illtreating, a pony belonging to him by causing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state. P. S. Jones stated that about half-past twelve noon on the 3rd inst., he was on duty at Astmoor Bridge, Halton. He saw the defendant's horse drawing a trap containing two ,calves and a number of bags, in charge of a youth named William Worrall. As the animal was in poor condition and appeared to be in pain, he examined it and he discovered underneath the saddle an old raw wound, abolit the size of a crown piece. The wound was discharging matter. Inspector Aplin, R.S.P.C.A. corroborated.—The defendant who said he did not think the horse was near se bad as it was, was fined 40s and costs, lOs 6d. WWI DESERTION AT WlDNES.—Michael Quinn, a labourer, at Widnes Alkali Works, was summoned before the Widnes Magistrates, .on Thursday, to answer a charge of deserting his wife Julia, and refusing to main- tainher.—Thecomplainant saideince shehadbeenmarried to the defendipit he had carried on "something scanda- lous." He had continually illtreated her, and had deser- ted her on no less than five occasions. Three weeks ago he removed his clothes and furniture from the house, and had said that he would not maintain her until he was compelled. He was able to earn £2 per week.— Annie Brannon, of Anne-st., said she had lited opposite the parties. The defendant had treated his wife bar- barously.—The defendant said the furnace at which he worked was now stopped, and he was a labourer at 3s 6d per day. He was willing to live with his wife again.— The Renal ordered the defendant to contribute 7s per week towards his wife's support.—The defendant said he could not pay so much. He was justified in leaving her as she threatened to poison him. A VIOLENT SOLDIER AT RUNCORN. John Griffiths, a rough-looking fellow' was brought before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Davies, at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, charged with'haying used obscene and profane language, and also with assaulting P.C, Ratcliffe.— About nine o'clock on Saturday night Constable Ratcliffe received a complaint from two gentlemen that the prisoner was using most disgusting language in Church-at., and on proceeding there he found their statements were true. He took the prisoner into custody, but he behaved ee violently that Constables Ratcliffe and Gibson had the utmost difficulty in taking him to the police station. A strngee of several minutes' duration took plase on the ground, and Ratcliffe was itruck on the chest and other parts of the body. When searched a pair of drawers and a shirt, together with a quantitT of bread and a few coppers, were found upon the prisoner.—With the glib- ness of tongue of an eld hand, the prisoner made a long statement to the magistrates. He said he had served her Majesty 14 years in India and North America, and he knew better than to use vile and slanderous language. He asked to be discharged as that was the first time he had been in that court.—Supt. Hollingworth said the prisoner had recently been convicted for assaulting the police at Dukinfield. His conduct in the cells was most violent. —The prisoner, in default of paving a total sum of £2 3s 4d, was sentenced to six weeks' hard labour.

THE WATCH ROBBERY AT WIDNES CENTRAL I At Widnes Petty Sessions, en Thursday, before Mr. T. Sutton Timsnis, a good-looking young German, named ' Leo Ahrenfeldt, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the 25th June last year, stolen from the ' Central Hotel, Widnes, a watch and chain, the property of Harriett Vickers, the waitress, and also a watch and chain and a revolver, the property of Albert Edward Wilson. At the time in question the prisoner took up his residence for several days, and conducted himself as a gentleman of means with a most important business to attend to. His real character was not discovered until Saturday, the 25th June, when he suddenly disappeared, without paying his bill. Strangely enough, the watches and chains were also son est, but inquiries revealed that the prisoner had pledged the ladies' watch and guard at Crewe, and the gentleman's at Birmingham. A few days later he was apprehended at Windsor on a charge of de- frauding an hotel keeper, and was sentenced to six months' hard labour. At the end of this period he was again arrested and sentenced to a further term of three months for committing an hetet robbery at Osferd. On Thursday he appeared before Mr. Timmis to answer for his misdeeds at Widnes. Since the rolsbery Mr. Wilson, the owner of the watch, who was employed at the works of Messrs. Mathieson and Co., had died, but his brother, Matthew Verity Wilson, bank agent, Leeds, identified the articles. The prisoner said he had com- mitted the theft because ha was in difficulties and hard up. He had already been pneished to the exteueof ten months' imprisoninent.—He wa.s committed to take his trial at the County Quarter Sessions. As the prisoner ' could not speak English, the services of an interpreter— Wm. Frost, of Duke-st., Liverpool—were employed._

_ ANOTHER WOUNDING _ CASE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. T. Sutton Tim- ruis and Mr. J. Brock, Patrick Costello, a powerful man, was brought up on remand charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm upon John Connolley. It appeared that the men earn a living a.s chemical labourers, and lodge at the same house, 44, Wellington-st. On Saturday afternoon the prisoner and the landlady had a quarrel, which terminated in the woman being ejected into the back yard. Connolley, who had been lying on a sofa in another room, then took the woman's part, and told the prisoner that he ought not to harm her. The prisoner retorted that he would have none of his interference. and, seizing a pint beer bottle, he struck Connolley a blow on the head that smashed the bottle into many pieces, and inflicted a serious wound. Blood flowed most profusely, and whilst he was bathing his head, the prisoner again attacked him, striking him several times on the face with his clenched hand. The prisoner than took up a spade that was near the fire place, and threa- tened to kill Connolley before he left the house. A woman named Mary Ann McMullen now interposed and suc- ceeded in obtaining possession of the spade' and the pri- soner was given into custody. Mary Costello the landlady, who is a widow, said the prisoner hat:l:been "keeping company" with'her. Dr. Hutchinson deposed that he had attended Connolley, who had a wound an inch long on the upper left side of the head, penetrating to the bone. There were also a number of small skin wounds on his face. P.C. Holbrook said he apprehended the prisoner, who in reply to the charge stated, "Yea, I did it; he should interfere in his own affairs." The prisoner now pleaded guilty to using the bottle, but added that he did not intend to hurt Connolley. He was committed to take his trial at the next Quarter Ses- sions.

GENEELL ELLIOT HOTEL BOWLING GREEN, I Cucurr.—The opening of the above bowling green , for the season took place on Saturday afternoon, when there was a good attendance. The green was in splendid condition, and a number of games hav- ing been played, the green was declared open. Sides having been chosen a local game was played. After- wards a substantial supper was given by the pro- prietor to the players, visitors, and friends to the I number upwards of 30, and a convival evening was spent. • TowN COUNTIES. "The county Government Review" says :—" The following is a complete list of the towns and cities which it is proposed by various members shall be added to the counties to be created 'under the Local Government Bill : York, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Kingston-on-Hull, Not- tingham, Bristol, Chester, Lincoln, Worcester, Gloucester, Exeter, Southampton. Cardiff, Burnley. Salford, Preston, Walsall, Derby, Northampton, Swan.ea, Rochdale, Croyaon, St. Helens, Hudders- field, Bath, Stockport, Wigan, Birkenhead, and War- rington." SWINE FEVER.—An area comprising the Runcorn Police Division has been notified as being infected with swine fever. The infected area consists of the townships of Acton Grange, Anderton, Antrobus, , Appleton-with-Hull, Aston Grange, Aston-by-Sut- -1 ton-with-Middleton Grange, Barnton, Bartington, Great Budworth, Clifton, Comberbach, Cogshall, Dutton, Daresbury, Grappenhall, Halton; Hatton, Kekewich, Latchford. (the part outside the borough of Warrington), Little Leigh, Morbury, Moore, Nor- ton. Preston-on-the-Hill, Runcorn, Seven Oaks, Stockham, Stretton, Sutton, Walton Inferior, Walton Superior. Weston, Whitley Inferior, and Whitley Superior.

COUNCILLOR JOSEPH SHAW GREEN, Warrington, has just been appointed a Fellow of the Royal Sta- tistical Society, of which Mr. Goschen, the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer is President. TEMPERANCE MEETING AT MOORB.—The last of the winter series of temperance meetings was held in the Moore Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Thursday evening, when there was a large attendance. Several interesting addresses were delivered and a petition was, at the close of the meeting, agreed to and ordered to be sent to Mr. Caine, M.P. for Barrow, protesting against the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill. DOWN THE RIVER. The first sail of the season was made from Warrington on Satarday, and there was quite a lively company of boats. Mr. John Peers, in charge of the Woodcock, took the lead from Atherton Quay SOOR after one o'clock, and kept it to the journey's end at New Ferry. The Maggie 'got along admirably, and might have got the lead had it not been that she lost time by acting as a good Samaritan. One party on a email steamer were helpless in consequence of an accident with the fan. The Maggie came to their assistance. and took them aboard. Two other boats grounded off Halton Marsh, the tide being n light one, but the May-Fly and Florence were amongst those that were successful in going the full length of the journey. A wrecked brigantine, the Dun- leery, was a striking object off Frodsham score. It was being towed down the river from Weston when it grounded opposite Ince, and could not af- terwards be got afloat. The vessel was one of 400 tons, and had a cargo of rock salt for New- castle.

THE PRESENCE OF MINERS' AGENTS AT IN- QUESTS. —fr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, St. Helens, has written to Mr. Henry Matthews, Home Secretary, asking if it was necessary for a miners' agent, before he could attend an inquest on behalf of the men, to obtain the written consent of the majority of the miners; and also whether it would . .

not meet the requirements of the Co-al ifine-e; keit; lation Act, 1887, if all men in a miners' agent dis- trict met and gave a 'written appointment to their agent to attend all inquests held on the bodies of colliers dying from injuries received in a coal mine. He has received the following reply: —" I am directed by the Secretary of State to ac- knowledge the receipt of your letter of the 4th instant, asking for information in regard to sub- section 8 of the 48th section of the Coal Mines Regulation Act, 1887, and I am to warn you that he cannot give decisions on points of law or interpret Acts of Parliament, nor are his decisions binding, but he is of opinion that the Act-does require that a person claiming to attend an inquest as represent- ing the workmen should be appointed for that lour- pose by the orper in writing of the majority of the workmen employed at the mine in which a fatal accident has occurred. The workmen employed can meet, and if the majority concur in an appoint- , ment, the order making such appointment can be reduced to writing by any person authorised by such majority to act for them in that behalf.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, GODFRay LIISHINGTON." MEATH or o prie OF THE MEN.--Wifflain Lunt, of Derby-square, Prescot, one of the six men injured in the recent gas explosion in the Lea Green Colliery, near St. Helens, died on Saturday. It will be remem- bered that Thomas Lunt, the father of deceased, and John Lunt, his brother, were also injured, so that Dr. Gaskell has had three patients in the one house. No hopes of the recovery of William were enter- tained from the first, but the fact of his death has caused an additional shock to the injured father and to the family. He was 26 years of age. The other men who live in St. Helens are progressing favour- ably, Mr, F, Smith, coroner for the Manor of Pres- Cot, Opened an inquiry at the Royal Hotel, Prescot, on Monday night, into the circumstances attending ' the death of William Lent. John Lunt identified the bedy as that of his brother, who, with witness and their father, and three other men, were working in the Potato Delph Mine, at Lea Green, on the 4th inst. A fall of roof was expected, and they had all retired for a time to rest. A fall soon afterwards took place, and a quantity of gas was set free, which was ignited by its coming in contact with the candle belonging to witness's father, and which was fixed to a pack about a yard from the roof, and twenty . yards from the fall. An explosion followed. They were all burned, but deceased sustained the most serious injuries. He died on Saturday. In reply to the coroner, witness said naked lights had always been used in the Potato Mine while he had worked in it, but in the next seam safety lamps were used. The inquiry was ai.journed for a week. ANTI-VACCINATioN PROCREDINGS.—At the New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday. before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale, Joshua Richardson, of Earlestown, was summoned by Mr. Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer, for neglec- ting to have his child vaccinated. The case had been adjourned from the last court owing to a mis- take in filling up the dates on a doctor's certificate. Mr. Daniel Garnett again appeared on behalf of the defendant, and, in reply to the magistrates' clerk, said he was not an agent for the Anti-Vaccination Society. He was not the secretaiy ot the society, but he was a personal friend of the defendant, who had instructed him to appear on his behalf. He handed up the Bench the doctor's certificate alluded to, which had been altered, and the proper dates inserted. I'a reply to Mr. Gillespie, Mr. Garnett said Dr. Patterson had made the alterations.—Mr. Gillespie pointed out that he had not initialled the alterations, and they had no evidence before them that he had altered the figures.—The Chairman (Mr. Houghton) said the Bench could not recognise that certificate, and adjourned the case until next court day for a fresh certificate to be obtained.--Wm. Grimshaw, of Rarlestown, was summoned for fail- ing to have two of his children vaccinated.—Defen- dent pleaded guilty, and said he had a. reasonable excuse for not having the children vaccinated. He had his first three children vaccinated, the third of which still suffered. The child's arms, legs, and body, he said, were one mass of sores, and had been so ever since it was vaccinated over two yeurs ago. The child had been under the doctor ever since, and he had just received a heavy doctor's bill. He was I coesequently afraid of having his two youngest children vaccinated —Mr. A. Cooper said he had brought that case before Mr. Sutton, the clerk to Guardians, and asked if those circumstances might be considered a reasonable excuse. Mr. Sutton told him no—he must take the case and leave it to the Bench.—The Bench made an order with regard to the first child for it to be vaccinated, and in the second case imposed a fine of 5s and costs, the Chairman remarking that the law m ust be carried out.

NORTHWICH DIVISION LIBERA.L ASSOCIATION AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. A special meeting of the Executive Committee of the Northwich Division Liberal Association, was held at the office of Mr. A. Fletcher, at Northwich, on Saturday afternoon, for the purpose of cnsider- iug the report of a sub-committee on the local Government Bill.—Mr. G. H. Deakin occupied the chair.—The report was submitted by Mr. W. Hand- ley, the secretary, and having been slightly amended was adopted as follows We approve with satisfaction the proposed creAtion of County and District Governing Authorities and their election by ballot on a wide and popular suffrage as a wise and necessary step of decentralisation, but are of opinion that County Councils should have the full control land direct management of all County police and magis- terial business, and that the proposed joint or dual con- trol should be strongly objected to. We are of opinion that the County Council should have full control and management of county, police, and Hundred rating, adopting as the basis or standard the valuation made for Poor law purposes, but to insure uni- formity of rateable assessment, the deductions as between gross and rateable value should be pro rata the same throughout the county, as provided in the Valuation Metropolic Acts. We are of opinion that all members of county and licensing authorities should be directly representative and elected by the ratepayers, including the filling up of casual vacancies. Also—

That the position of chairman of county council should in itself qualify him as a. County Justice. Also— That the whole of the Licensing Clauses should be carefully watched, that compensation for non-renewal of a license should be uncompromisingly objected to, and that adequate provision should be made for the fullest expression of public opinion of every local district, in- cluding the right of appeal to the Licensing Committee and County Council. Also— That the proposed contribution of fourpence per head for indoor paupers should include the children of widows or orphans livins with their relatives if in receipt of Out- door relief. Also—

That all members of District Councils should be elected by the ratepayers (provided that casual vacancies only be fate. Ly co-optation) and that after the first election the chairman or other deputed member of such District Council should be the returning officer. Also— That Rural District Councils should be the Highway authority in their respective districts and have the same powers to compel the making of the necessary roads or streets as now possessed by Urban Authorities. Also— That allowances to District Councils for maintenance of main roads should be equal to that hitherto allowed by County and Government. Also— That the rates levied for maintenance of Cemeteries where hitherto borne by the Poor rate should be on the same basis of rateable value.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By "Anizt."

I heard of a curious thing in the way of coinci- dences, the other day, in connection with a well- known Runcorn family. There is nothing strange in the first fact that the father was born on the 28th December, but his eldest son appeared in this vale of tears on the same date (of course, in a later year), and the natal hour of that son's eldest son occurred also on the 28th December. And further, the age of the paternal parents was 23 years when each of these events occurred. The Runcorn pilots, who are an able and deserv- ing body of men, have got a very serious grievance at the present time. For some years nest, business has been particularly brisk with them, and now the i bad trade s being aggravated by the encroachments of the Liverpool pilots, two of whom have, even during the past week, steered vessels to Runcorn. Of course, in doing so these men are breaking no law. Up to Liverpool, pilotage is compulsory; above it is optional, but the winding nature of the deep, and its frequent changes render navigation very difficult and makes it absolutely necessary. that a pilot should be aboard any vessel of impor- tance. Here lies the rub. The Liverpool pilots are un- acquainted with the up?er reaches of the river and it is only by assuming a knowledge that they can- not possess thac a captain trusts his vessel in their charge. They, in turn, place dependence upon the steam packet that ia towing the ship and in Provi- dence, for were the hawser to part, or the packet break down, they wouid be hopelessly at sea, and much damage might be the result. There's honour amongst thieves they say, and certainly there ought to be a little &writ de corps amongst pilots. Let the Liverpool men keep to the track that they under- stand and can navigate, and not venture into un- known waters in a very spirit of greediness, and to the injury of the properly qualified pilots. Mr. Handley, the energetic secretary to the North- wich Division Liberal Association, has just brought his winter's lecturing campaign to a close. In his own constituency and the neighbouring division of Eddisbury he has delivered no less than 17 lectures upon the subject of Ireland.and thousands of people have now a better knowledge of "Ireland, its natural beauties lout history, and present misery" than they had before. The facts narrated by Mr. Handley, and the scenes lie described, were forcibly impressed upon the mind by the admirable series of lime light views displayed by his son Ur. Horace Handley. It is impossible to over-estimate the value of this pleasant mode of educating the people, and I hope that next autumn Mr. Handley will deal with some other subject upon which public opinion needs ripening. Widuesians are constantly being told that if the atmosphere of the town is not exactly laden with Sabean odours from the spicy shore Of Arable the blest, and the aspect of its streets and buildings is not aesthetically beautiful, yet they receive compensa- tion in the shape of slow death rate. I am beginning to think that that low death rate is a delusion and a snare. Welcome death, say I, if one is to live in fear and dread of the impending stroke. And these con- tinued reports of the outbreak of typhoid fever and scarlet fever are certainly most disquieting, whilst measles are not without their terrors. At the last monthly meeting of the Local Board, for in- stance, the Medical Officer reported six fresh cases of typhoid fever, and left the public in doubt as to how many cases of old standing there were, and It is a problem I have not been able to solve. All the same,,l do not think there is at present much cause for alarm. The town possesses a good hospital, the Board is pushing forward the completion of the sewerage scheme, and at the head of the Health Committee is Mr. Carey, a most energetic and cap- able gentleman. I heard a whisper yesterday that it is intended to elevate several local gentlemen on the commis- sion of the peace of the county. The redoubtable doctor has been several times mentioned in this con- nection, and doubtless his devotion and services to the Unionist cause will be recognised by the dignity of J.P. being conferred upon him.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MRTHITCHEN, RUNCORN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MRTHITCHEN, RUNCORN.

Much grief and astonishment was expressed in Runcorn on K ednesday, when it became known that Mr. T. 11. Hitchen, :solicitor, Bank Chambers, Runcorn, had died suddenly at his residence, at Frodsham, that morning. On the 3rd instant Mr. Hitchen met with an accident, by which he severely sprained his ankle, and he had since been confined to his room. The injury was ittended to by Dr. Weaver, and no suspicion was entertained that the patient also suffered from any serious bodily ailment. On Tuesday night he was in the best of spirits and apparently in the best of healths and he retired to rest about eleven o'clock. At half- past three next morning he awoke and complained of a severe pain in the stomach, and the symptoms were so serious that Mrs. Hitchen in her alarm caused one of the servants to call in Mr. M. G. Linaker, a neighbour. That gentleman did all in his power to relieve the sufferer, but without avail, and Mr. liitchen expired in a few brief min- utes. The deceased gentleman, who had only at- tained the age of 37 years, was the son of the late Major Hitchen, of Newton Hall, Frodsham. Des- igned for the legal profession he served his articles with Mr. John Ashton, clerk to the magistrates, Run- corn; and on being admitted became the partner of Mr. W. H. Linaker, of that town. For the last eight years, I however, he had practised his profession on his own ac- count, and by his kindly and genial demeanour he had made for himself a host of friends In politics he was a Conservative, and until a few weeks ago, when he re- signed the position, he was the secretary to the Frod- sham branch of the Primrose League. He was also an active member of the Ancient Order of Freemasons, and at the time of his death was enjoying the confidence of his brethren in the position of W.M., the highest honour his lodge could confer upon him. He leaves a widow an two children to mourn his loss.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

The inquest upon the body was opened yesterday - morning, at the .Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsham, by Mr. EL. Churton, coroner. Mr. C. E. Linaker was the foreman of the jury. The relatives of the deceased were repro- - seated by Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, and Pr. Tafior,,.. of Chester. appeared on behalf of the Accident Insurance - Company, by whom the life of the deceased was insured. The Coroner said the simple duty of the jury was to satisfy themselves as to the cause of death; they had nothing whatever to do with any insurance company. Dr. Weaver deposed that at midnight on the 3rd. Inst. he visited the residence of the deceased, in response to a summons, and found him suffering from a severe sprain at the ankle. There was no dislocation and no fracture. He attended to the injury. At that time the deceased was well in his bodily health, but two days later he - complained of a derangement of his digestion, and he (witness) prescribed for him. In the course of his attendance he did not find the deceased suffering -from any ailment likely to cause sudden death. He•was not in a position to assign the cause of his very, sudden death without making a post-mortem examination. The Coroner at once adjourned the inquiry for two • hours, to allow D. Weaver to make the necessary ex- amination. Upon the resumption of the inquiry, Dr. Weaver de- posed that he had made a post mortem examination of the body of the deceased. There was discolouration and a slight swelling at the injured ankle of the left foot. On opening the chest he found that the lungs were in a congested state, and also that the pulmonary artery be- tween the heart and the lungs was completely stopped up . by a large clot of blood. This clot extended from the heart into the branches of both lunge. This was the - cause of death. On further examination he discovered that the viens in the neighbourhood of the injured ankle • and behind the knee were in an inflamed state, and a detached clot of blood from this vein must have caused the obstruCtion in the artery of the heart. There was a fracture of the ankle joint. He was of opinion that the original injury to the ankle was really and truly the cause of death. The heart was free from disease; in face was quite sound. Dr. Taylor said Dr. Robinson and himself were willing to corroborate everything Dr. Weaver had said.
Mr. H. G. Linaker hiving given evidence as to the manner in which Mr. Hitchen died,
The jury, after a brief consultation in private,returned a verdict of "Accidental death," in accordance with the medical testimony.

HOW THE ACCIDENT OCCURRED. Although witnesses were in attendance at the inquest ready to describe how Mr. llitchen received his accident the coroner either forgot or did not think it necessary to call this evidence. Our representative ascertained that on the evening of the 3rd inst. Mr. and Mrs. Hitchen paid a complimentary visit to Mr. John Weston, who is in charge of the Weston section of the Manchester Ship Canal,. and who has recently resided at Alvanley-terrace, Frodsham. As Mr. and Mrs. Hitchen were about to take their departure at ten o'clock, a fall of hailstones and snow occurred, and they were induced to extend their visit some time longer. Upon leaving later Mr. Ffitchen safely descended the steps leading into the house, but , slipped upon the pavement, and fell with his foot awk- wardly doubled boneath him. Besides a slight fracture- d the ankle, the foot was dislocated, but Mr. Weston cleverly restored the bones to their normal position, and Mr. Ilitchen was taken home, and the doctor sum. . moned. The melancholy end to so simplq an aocident- is already known.

div.head: AN EDITOR INVESTIGATES.
div.p: AN EDITOR INVESTIGATES.

The Tunbridge Wells "Courier" of April 20th says :—" We are aware that many people are scep- tically inclined towards patent medicines and adver- tisements of them, but few more striking instances -of the advantage of keeping a bona fide specific con- tinually before the public notice can be referred to than the success which has attended Warner's SAFB Cure, of world-wide fame. This has been success- fully kept under the notice of the people of this dis- trict for some time, and as if to clinch the argu- ments which have been periodically adduced, some very striking local testimonials have just been given. Local testimonials are facts that cannot very well be got rid off, and should' afford a valuable stimulus to Messrs. Warner's specifics in this district. A well-known gentleman, the representative of a large business depot in the town, called on us the other day, and observing that he had given an eulogistic testimonial of Warner's SAFE Nervine, published in our last issue. we interrogated him on the subject, for, unlike some of our contemporaries, we have always been chary of what medical advertisements find a place in our columns. Mr. Brunker's reply (for that is the gentleman to whom we allude), was even more eulogistic of Warner's specifics than his testimonial, of which he remarked that he did not think to say half what he might have done when it -occurred to hi,.i to write it. Mr. Brunker's was evidently an extreme case, as he had failed in a neighbouring town where he had formerly resided to obtain relief from four doctors, but the particular specific of Messrs. Warner, -which he got from a chemist when other remedies failed, acted, te use his own words, "like magic." As this matter has come under our personal observation, we feel it may be of interest to our readers who have per- used Messrs. Warner's advertisement in our columns. Editorial comment like the above is valuable because it is unsolicited. It proves that the remedy mentioned has merit, and that the testimonials given by people who • have been benefited by its use are true and will stand investigation. Local testimonials, like the ones referred to by the editor of the "Courier," have been published in cities and towns throughout the United Kingdom. They are the plain, unvarnished statements of friends • and neighbours whose health has been restored or whose lives have been saved by means of the remedies which they so thankfully praise. They are ' worth volumes of fine-spun theories, because they are the practical evidences of the great value of the medi- cines of which they speak—evidences which have sprung from the lips of sincere and grateful men and 'women, and as such are entitled to the respect and confidence of those who read them. A better verification of the state- ments made by the proprietors of Warner's Sere Cure, that they have a sovereign remedy for all diseases of the kidallys, liver, and urinary organs could not be asked for. This great medicine can be had of all chemists at 4s 6d per bottle, or direct of H. El. Warner and Co., 86, Clerkenwell-road, London, E.C.

and C. Lister. DRUNKENNESS.—John Zechariah Zadock, of Warring- ton was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Warring- ton, on the sth May. REFUSING TO QUlT.—Thomas Bourke, a labourer liv- ing at Lymm, was charged with having been drunleand refusing to quit the licensed premises of Thomas Marsh' at Lymm, on the 28th April. Defendant did not appear, but Mr. Marsh stated that when be asked Bourke to leave his house the latter turned round and struck him. A fine of 3s and costs was imposed. KILLING Dtruss.—John Winstanley, farmer, Lying., was charged with having unlawfully and maliciously killed two ducks on the 27th April, the property of Good- man Green. Mr. Welford, solicitor, appeared on behalf of the defendant. It appeared from the evidence that defendant had complained to Green alont the latter's fowl trespassing on his land, and on the day named he shot at three young ducks which were ifi his field, killing one and injuring the other two, one of which subse- quently died. Although the ducks were only ten days old, complainant put their value at 10s, they being, he stated, of a fine breed. Mr. Welford contended that de- fendant was justified in his action and quoted an ana- lagous case which had come before a superior court in support of the contention. The Bench, however, deci- ded that Mr. Winstanley was not justified in the course he hadtaken, and ordered him to pay 5s damage, 5s fine, and to pay costs.

div.head: NORTHWICH AND THE WEAVER TRUST.
div.p: NORTHWICH AND THE WEAVER TRUST.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Northwich Local Board on Tuesday night, the Clerk (Mr. Cow- ley) read a printed circular from Mr. H. Linaker, Clerk to the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, con- taining a copy of a report which he had made to the Guardians of dist Union on the Bth inst., in which he drew attention to a question recently put to the President of the Board of Trade in the House of Commons by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., having reference to the River Weaver Trust, "which might seriously affect the interests of the ratepayers of the county." Having read the circular; the Clerk said it simply meant—would the Board pass a resolution protesting against Northwich being benefitted ? (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. Williams thought they ought to express an opinion quite the contrary to that given by Mr. Linaker. He moved that the communication be referred to the General Purposes Committee.—Mr. Worsley :1 think Mr. Brunner is perfectly right in what he has done, and I shall second Mr. Williams' proposition.—Mr. Brandreth : I have great pleasure in' supporting the resolution.—The motion was then unanimously agreed to.

div.head: MACCLESFIELD GUARDIANS.
div.p: MACCLESFIELD GUARDIANS.

At the weekly meeting of the Guardians of Maccles- field Union, on Tuesday,. the circular letter from the Run- corn Board of Guardians, in reference to the-attitude of Mr. Brunner, M.P., and the surplus revenue paid by the River Weaver Trust to. the Cheshire city rate, was con- sidered. The Clerk (Mr. J. F. May), after reading tke document, said its purport was that the Runcorn Board desired the Macclesfierd Guardians to join their protest against any scheme such as Mr. Brunner proposed, which would divert the £15,000 paid annually to the county rate to the sole benefit of the Northwich salt trade Mr. C. E. Therneycroft, J.P., a member of the trust, said Mr. Brunner wanted to take the money from the county ratepayers to benefit the salt trade of North- wich, which was new very insignificc,rit. Mr. Carr moved that the Guardians join in the protest of the Run- corn Board. The Chairman (Mr. Hordern) seconded the motion, which was adopted.
