div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1888. THE SHIP CANA.L WORKS,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1888. THE SHIP CANA.L WORKS,
A WIDNES MAN SENTENCED TO THE "CAT."

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Day,Jarees Daniels (29), a ship carpenter, was brought up for sentence on a charge of having, at Widnes, on the 10th March, robbed Mary Maguire of 28, and also assaulted her. Three otherprisoners who had been convicted of similar offences, were also placed in the dock. His lordship sd these prisoners stood convicted of offences whicll he was able to deal with in a way different from that which he was compelled to deal with those guilty of other offences. He was able to shorten the terms of their imprisonment and yet inflict upon the prisoners adequate punishment. He looked upon this pun- ishment as valuable for its reforming character. He had ascertained by careful inquiry among those able to judge that the punishment he was about to inflict did reform more than any other, and that men who were punished by it rarely returned to the offences for which they were so punished. There was no cruelty about it, and no substantial injury; but it was a sharp punishment , which criminals disliked and avoided, and never received a second time. The prisoners must under- stand that in sentencing them to these short terms of imprisonment it in no way represented the pun- ishment which their offences deserved. Daniels • was then sentenced to four months' imprisonment • and to receive ,twenty lashes with the "cat.' The other prisoneVs were dealt with in a similar manner.
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 18.-HALTON AND ITS CASTLE.
Halton—the Heletune of Doomsday Book--is so ileh in historic and antiquarian interest, that,, in addition to our account of last week of the changes that will probably take place in the township
through the making of the canal, we may in the present article take a cursory glance backwards over its annals, which have been very fully recorded in Mr.
Beamont's "History of the Castle of alton and the Priory or Abbey of Norton." H Norton, Sutton, Aston, and Weston derive their names from their relative geo-
graphical positions to the north, south, east, and
west, Halton is the high town—the "town upon the bill" of the district, its prefix being by one authority ascribed to the old, Eng- lish word for bill, " haw " oi "how," and by

others to "Allt" or "Alt," a hill or cliff. Halton does not seem to have cut any particitlar figure in Roman and Saxon timee, but its singularly commanding eminence soon attracted the strategic eye of the early Norman, and Nigel, who was made first baron in the time of the Conqueror, erected a
stronghold on the highest summit of the hill. Of this earliest castle it.is surniised that no part re-

mains, with the possible exception of a carved cor- bel, now in the Warrington Museum • The next holder of the barony, William Fitz - Nigel, was the founder of the religious house at Runcorn, Which, being afterwards removed, became the well-known Priory of Norton. This removal took place in the time of the third baron, William Fitz William, who, evidently having strong religious leanings, endowed the new priory with the tithes of his lands n Thel- wall, on condition that the monastics qffered up prayers and masses for himself and his family. William Fitz William, dying in Normandy without issue, was succeeded in the barony by Eustace Fitz John, the husband of his sister, who was also a great benefactor of religious foundation. Passing over two or three of the descendants of Eustace, we find that the "seventh baron was a notable warrior named Roger. A FALSTAFFIAN' ARMY. "

It is said that on one occasion, when this baron was at Chester fair, news came that the Earlßandle Blundeville was shut up and surrounded by the Welsh in Rhuddlan Castle, whereupon Roger collec- ' ted together all the musicians, singers, and beggars at the fair and marched to the earl's rescue. The Welshmen were impressed by the largeness of the host which was marching upon them, and not per- ceiving its unmilitary character, fell into a panic and made a precipitate and disorderly retreat. For this notable achievement Roger had very appropri- ately conferred upon him by the grateful earl the rule and government in I.erpetuity of all the musi- cians, singers, beggars, and idle strollers within the earldom. This baron in his after lite took part in many warlike scenes, amongst others that of the storming of Acre by Richard Cceur de Lion, and was in the end buried with great honours in the family burial place at Stanlaw. John Lacy. the son of Roger, was one of the Runnymede barons who ex- torted the greet charter from King John, and was also one of those chosen to see that the charter was faithfully obierved by the king. In 12113 he suf fered papal excommunication, apparently more in consequence of having incurred the .of the monarch, than because of any offence deserving so severe a censure, but nevertheless he afterwards held high offices in the State, and in 1232 he sec-. ceeded to the earldom of Lincoln. About this time we find that Halton is spoken of, or rather written of in the flexible spelling of those days as " Hathel-, ton," and that the privilege of .fishing in the Mer- sey throughout the: limits of Halton was worth a yearly acknowledgment of "sixpence, or a pair of spurs." The ninth baron of Halton, Edmund Lacy,' does notseemto have distinguished himself in any way except it he in allowing himself to be married, with- out his own consent, to a Provencal lady, a relative of the reigning queen. The tenth earl, Henry de Lacy, on the other hand, took a prominent part in State affairs, and he led the van in the great battle against the Scotch at Falkirk. This great noble- 'man seems to have had little personal acquain- tance with his barony of Halton, as he spent a large part of his time in London. The house in which he lived was known as "Lincoln's Inn," and afterwards fell into the hands of the lawyers and has since been one of their most celebrated resorts. MEDIEVAL LAWLESSNESS. Henry diedwitbout male issue, but his daughter having married Thomas of Laneaster, of the Royal House of Plantagenet, the latter succeeded in her right as the eleventh baron of Halton. In the time of Thomas of Lancaster the neighbourhood of Hal- ton seems to have been infested with lawless charac- ters, and even the castle was broken into and rob- bed by a band of robbers under the leadership of a William de Huxley. The unenviable reputation of the district in this respect has lea a historian to ascribe to the local Halton a passage in Langland's famous medieval poem "Piers Plowman's Vision," which says that Thom the pass at Haulton Peverte may pass without fear of robbynge, thus insinuat'ng that "poverte," was the only thing that could escape-the rapacity of tie outlaws of the 'district. According to Mr. Beamont, however, it was proved by Dr. Kendrick, of Warrington, that Langland's , reference wes not to the Cheshire " Haulton" but to a pass at Alton, on the borders of Surrey and Hampshire. Thomas of Lancaster, having made an unsuccessful rising against the Xing his estate's were forfeited for treason, and in 1323 Halton was honoured by a visit of the reigniag monarch. Edward 11, who stopped there from the Ist to the 3rd of November. ANCIENT LAND TENURES.

In the succeeding reign the attainder of Thomas of Lancaste; was reversed, and his brother, Henry of Lancaster, succeeded to his possessions, and was the twelfth baron of Halton. About this time an inquisition on Halton was made, from which we find that it was estimated to be worth 148 Oa 200 in the money of the period. We are further told that "there is a certain castle there built with a stone wall embattled, which, in time of peace, costs more than it yields, unless the lord there shall be in possession of it. And the pasture of the same castle cannot be extended, because it is common, up to the walls, to all the tenants of the town of Hal- ton." Mention is also made of a "several pasture called Astmore, worth by the year 9s; and one windmill and two watermills, worth by the year,, deducting reprises,. %8 Bd." The thirteenth baron was also a Henry of Lancaster, surnamed in his youth " Wryneck," and in his old age "The. good Duke of Lancaster.' This miner of Halton seems to have been both pious and litigious. His piety is attested by a kind of confessional and penitential/ book, entitled "Mercy, Gramercy," to the writing of which he devoted much of his leisure, while we find traces of litigiousness in the exlensive, claims he put forward in a legal suit he was engaged in. Amongst these claims, is a right to have a prison at Halton; to have his burgesses free of all tolls throughout the county of Chester; to take stallage of all chapmen at Halten, Runcorn, Weston, Daresbury, Norton, Moore, Acton Grange, Higher and Lower Walton, Appleton, Thelwall, Stretton," and numerous other places in, this part of Cheshire, and to have the channel of the Mersey free and kept open for a barge of eight oars be- tween Freshpool and his fishery at Thelwall. He also claimed a right to behead all thieves who con- fessed their offence. Among the rents which were paid to this Duke was one shilling,from Adam Cla- yton, for his tenement in Thelwall, in lieu of a pair of stag leather gloves furred with fox-akin; two shillings from Nether Walton, for the liberty of taking salmon in the Mersey at Lady Day; and sixpence for a pair of white spurs from William Mebberley, for his lands in Plumley. John of Gaunt, the patron of Chaucer, and the protector of Wycliffe, next succeeded to the possession of Hal- ton, by virtue of his marriage with Blanche. the daughter of the "good Duke." Gaunt made Halton his occasional hunting seat, and he is credited with having enlarged and improved the castle, and, ac- cording to Mr. Beamont, "the popular voice as- cribes to John of Gaunt the name of the neighbour- ing Fiddlers Ferry, in Cuerdley, which it is said was given to it after he had once passed over it with a party of stringed musicians, probably to exa- mine the ancient earth-works on the adjoining marsh." The son of John of Gaunt, Henry Bolingbroke, naturally succeeded to the barony of Halton, and on Bolingbroke's ascension to the English throne as Henry IV, Halton was merged with the Crown possessions, and from this time its history loses much of its local interest. In course of time the castle became the local Bastille, first for religious

recusants, and afterwards for malefactors of a meaner sort ; but in the time of Charles I. it was still able to stand a siege of several weeks by the Parliamentarians. After this it was dismantled, and began to fall into the decay in which it now' stands.
(To be Continued-)
EASTHAM.

Blasting operations have commenced at Eastham and there is work for quarrymen. The stone will be utilised in building an embankment for the canal. Two more steam navvies have been erected, bringing the total on this section to ten, and thirty more huts are being built. A great part of the section has been fenced in. Amongst other things a steam hammer has been added to the forge, a large pump has been erected in the yard, a brick field has been started on the spa- bank, and a large cement shed capable of holding LOW tons is being erected here. Telephonic communication is being made between Eastham and Ellesmere Port and will soon be complete, and the postal authorities are aolding a tele- graphic station to the Eastham Post Office: A collection was the other day made on this section for afitternamed Gambrial, who had lost both feet in an accident, and it 'realised £l4. Those at work on this section are making arrangements for passing away their spare time to as great an advantage as possible, and a glee party and minstrel troupe are being formed. It is also proposed, and the suggestion is a good one, to arrange a system of visits to different sections on Saturday afternoons and Sundays. -

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LITE MR. W. G. CUNNINGHAM,
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LITE MR. W. G. CUNNINGHAM,

The mortal remains of Mr. William Goodall Cunningham were interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Monday afternoon. The deceased gentleman, who had attained the advanced age of 71 years, was born at Macclesfield, but had for the past 35 years been a resident of Runcorn. For many years he had carried on atrextensive business as a draper, in Bridge-st., but in later years he employed himself as a commission agent. At one part of his career Mr. Cunningham took an active and prominent part in public affairs, and was a member of the Board of Commissioners Board of Guardians, and Burial Board. He performed much valuable work, and, if for no other reason, his memory should be kept green for the part he took in securing the footway across Runcorn Bridge. When the collective wisdom of the Board of Commissioners was at fault, he stepped into the breach, and -by his energy and address secured an advantage for the town that, it is said, would otherwise have been lost. In religion Mr. Cunningham was a Churchman, and had ful- filled the office of superintendent at Holy Trinity School for many years; while in politics he was a staunch Liberal and follower of Mr. Gladstone. He was always ready to give a reason for the faith that was in him, and he was delighted when he could break a lance with an opponent or discuss the weighty affairs of state with a friend. For the past two years he has been in failing health, but he re- tained the powers of his intellect to the last. As a mark of respect to his memory, the flag at the Town Hall was hoisted half-mast, and as the funeral pro- cession passed through the town blinds were drawn at many of the dwellings, and the shops were par- tiallyclosed. Preceding the hearse were Messrs. H. J. Grice, Thomas Kirkham, George Bell, Geo. Ward, and W. R. Wass. In the first mourning coach were Messrs. W. J. Cunningham and Allan Cunningham (sons), H. A. Hankinson (son-in-law), J. W. Light- burn, and Masters 11. and W. A. Hankinson (grand- sons). In the second were Messrs. W. Hankinson, John Cunningham. Ivan Cunningham, and B. Cun- ningham. The coffin was covered with numerous floral tributes. The burial service was impressively read by the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., Vicar of Holy Trinity. Mr. James Peck supplied the hearse and mourning coaches, and Mr. Caygill made the coffin.

Four steam nav--;rie-i—CTlt-13-e—Atne-rVa.n type are mew busily engaged on the section from Ellesmere Port to Ince, and the number of men employed is about 700". RUNCORN.

Four steam navvies of the American type are making great Progress on that part of the section nearest RUC), I corn, where the soil is admirably suited for excavating. There is a large spoil bank, about 15 to 20 feet high, at the centre of this section, on a piece of boggy land,whicls has sunk so much that only half of the spoil that has, ben deposited is now in view. Further on the section, nearer to Warrington. there is a very heavy clay to cut through. Three Priestman's dredgers are at work. These machines can be used for many purposes, and are , admirably adapted for the contractor's work. Only one man is required to work a dredger. There are three different types of the bucket or grab, to suit the various classes of material to be dealt with and these tools are made with capacities of three hinidredweight to three tons. The makers, a Hull firm, have supplied upwards of 400 of them to various firms, and have received a ilarge number of repetition orders, _

div.head: SECOND BILL
div.p: SECOND BILL

--- The Manchester Ship Canal Company recently presen- ted a petition to Parliament, praying forleave to deposit a second bill in Parliament enabling them to make im- portant alterations in theirworks at Manchester. It will be remembered that the late Sir Humphrey de Trafford strongly opposed any interference with that portion of his property known as the Home Farm, but successful negotiations have been entered into with the present baronet, by which the company have acquired a large ' portion of the property in question, thus enabling them greatly to improve the course of the canal at Manches- ter and Salford, and, to greatbr increase the accommoda- tion for wharfage purposes. It will also, have the effect of giving an independent access to the Manchester Docks, instead of only through the Salford Docks, as at present authorised. The question of dispensing with the stand- ing orders to enable the bill to be brought before Parlia- ment this session came on Tuesday before the Standing Orders Committee sf the House of Commons, Sir Tohn. Mowbray in the chair, and the committee decided that theprders should be dispensed with so as to allow the petition to be presented, and the bill proceeded with in the present session.

COMPANY, LIMITED. Lords Justices Cotton, Fry, and Lopes gave judg- me4,on Tuesday upon the appeal on behalf of the ordinary shareholders of this company from the de- cision of Mr. Justice North on the question of the principle on which the surplus assets should be dis- tributed. The undertaking had been purchased by the Manchester Ship CanaP Company, and the pur- chase money was sufficient to leave a very large surplus after the payment of all the debts of the Navigation Company and repaying to the share- holders the amounts they had paid on their shares. , The capital was divided into ordinary and prefer- ence shares, both of .ElO each, but while the former class had paid only .£3 lOs per share, the preference 'shares were fully paid up. The preference shares were entitled to a dividend of 5 per cent. out of the profits shown by the annual balance sheet before anything was pain tcrttre-orrlinary shareholders, but no priority was specifically given to them in the distribution of assets. ln those circumstances a summons was taken out by the voluntary liquida- tors for the purpose of obtaining a decision of the Court upon the question in what shares and propor- tions as between the holders of the preference and ordinary shares the balance ought to be distributed, and Mr. Justice North held that it should be divided pro rata according to the amounts paid up upon the shares.. From that decision Mr. Bircb,.who had been appointed to represent the interests of the ordinary shareholders, appealed, and submitted either that the preference shareholders -were entitiedto nothing more than the return of the amount of their shares, together with the 5 per cent. preference dividend secured by the resolution creating those shares, or that the ordinary shares•should,'by calls, be brought to an,equality with the preference shares,. and that then the surplus should be divided pro.ritca between all. Their lordships affirmed the decision of the court below, and dismissedthe appeal.. They, how- ever, held that the question was a proper subject Of appeal, and therefore allowed the costs to. come out of that portion of the fund that would be payable to the ordinary, shareholders, notwithstanding that these were stated to be shareholders who, although holding shares of both classes, had no•interest in the question.

ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER NEAR WARRINGTON. The Warrington borough police were early on 1 Thursday morning informed of the death of a farm labourer named Anthony Gibbon (48), which took place at midnight on Wednesday, under circum- stances of grave suspicion. The deceased wee a -native of Castlebar, county Mayo, and was in the employ of Mr: Thomas Hewitt, farmer, Lower Latch- ford, near Warrington. It is stated that on Satur- day evening he was drinking, in company with another labourer named Michael Garner, at the Rail- way Inn at Latchford. They left the house together, and reached the farm shortly after eleven o'clock. On arriving at the farm yard, it is alleged, a quarrel took place between them, in the course of which Garnet is said to have knocked hiscoinpanion down and kicked him several times in the stomach. The deceased afterwards went to bed in an outbuilding, and afterwards became ill. On Wednesday evening Dr. Spinks was called in, and some medicine was sent for, but Gibbon died a few hours after- wards.

, PRLSONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. At the Bbrough Court,. at Warrington, yesterday morn- ing, before-Dr. Gomall,„ Michael Garner, the man with whom the. deceased was drinking on Saturday, was brought up.in custody and charged with " having, on Saturday last, unlawfully killed and slain one-Anthony Gibbons, in Latchford, in the borough of Warrington." The circumstances of the case were narrated' by the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt). who said that the deceased, who was 48 years of age, was a farm labourer, and was' a native of Castlebar, county Mayo. He was a married man, and left a wife and family who, with the exception of one son, were-in Ireland. The son worked for Mr. Long, tanner, oflGrappenhali. The prisoner, who was 24 years of age was a farm labourer, and was a native of Galway. He and the deceased both worked for Mr. Thos. Hewitt, of Lower Wash-lane, Latchford, and slept in the ~‘ paddy" house. The deceased had worked for 'Mr-. Hewitt for about five weeks,. and the prisoner, who bore very good character, had worked for him for about twd'years. It appeared that the two men finished work, on Saturday evenin'g,and after doing so went to Grap- penha.ll, where they had a few glasses of beer at a public-- house. They subsequently returned to Latchford, and went to the Railway Inn + at aborat ten o'clock. After leaving the Railway Inn they went to the farm again. When they were near the stable door some words passed,. and the prisoner it was alleged, struck the deceased on the nose. The effect of the-blow was to cause the de- ceased to fall to the ground. From a statement made by the deceased, and taken. down shortly before his death, it would appear that the prisoner struck him, and also kicked him two or three times in the stomach and on the chest. After the. occurrence deceased was left lying on the ground, but he afterwards got up and joined the prisoner in the "paddy" house. On Sunday, at about noon, the deceased was walking about the yard., and Mr. Hewitt, who came to the 'yard, noticed thatte appeared as though.he was in pain. Presently. Gibbons accused the pnsonee of having kicked him several times in the stomach. In reply to the accusa- tion prisoner said Y I never kicked you; I did strike you and knock you down." He also made a charge against the deceased of having wanted to take 2s out of his pocket, which he was not going to let him have. Sunday,. Monday, and Tuesday passed, the deceased walking about, or remaining in bed in the " paddy " house, but doing no work. Mr. Hewitt saw that some- thing was the matter with him, and gave him suitable food. On WedntAday deceased appeared to be so much worse that Mr. Hewitt called in the policeman on the beat and told him. of the matter: Constable Harvey . _ .

'saw 'Mr. Garnett,the relieving officer, who visited the deceased, and afterwards Dr. Spinks was called in. He at once pronounced Gibbons' obe "in'a dying state, and the police were communicated With. -From enquiries made by them it was found that the prisoner had left on Wednesday morning to proceed to Boston, America. It had been 'known' for ten Or tWelve days pretioiiiily that he .was going to America, and -he had taken his passage. Gib-, bons .died about midnight on Wednesday, and on Thtirs- day morning Inspector Spinks --went to Liverpool, and with the assistance of Detective .Thornthwaite, of the Liverpool force, arrestcd the defendant on the S.S. I3oth- nia,. Inspector Spanks baiitioned 'him, ancl told him that he was accused of having caused the:death of An- thony Gibbons. Prisoner made reply—"l never did anything to him -; he has" been bad• all the week; I never kicked him,. but I did give him a fist on the nose." On arriving at the police station at Warrington, prisoner-Was formally' charged, and made a:statement that would be-ued an the hearisig of the case. What was now- desired was a remand.— Inspector Spinks then deposed to arresting the prisoner at Liverpool. He told the prisoner that he was a police inspector from Warrington, and had come to arrest him for causing the death of ' Ahthony Gibbons, at Lower Wash-lane, Latchford. Prisoner had booked in his pro- per name. His reply, after being cautioned, was , 1 never kicked him; Pgavebim,a, fist; on the nose, or on the face somewhere." When charged at Warrington he replied—" I did not kick him. I should not have touched him but I had a couple of shillings in my • pocket and he wanted to steal them frorn me. He was going tp strike me, and I struck him a fist on the -nose. That is all I have done to him. I offered to bring him twice to the Workhouse, or anywhere he wanted. He was right wough when I lefthim on Wednesday morning." The spector added that he saw Gibbons- at about 11-30 on Wednesday night. He asked him did he know that he was about to die, and deceased then made a statement which he signed in the presence. of witness.—Mr. White (magistrate's clerk) : That you:will produce at the pro- per time.—Prisoner said he had no reason to give why he should not be remanded, but he denied having kicked the deceased.—He was . remanded until Wednesday next.

LORD R. CHURCHILL AT PRESTO/T.—Lord Randolph ,Churchill,.M.P., addressing a gathering of about Eve thousand persons in the Public Hall, Preston, on Wed- nesday evening, said it could not be denied that order now reigned in Ireland, and that agitation was dying out. Rte regretted to announce that with regard to public expenditure he saw very little progress being ,made in retrenchment. The field of administrative reform was almost untouched. The majority of the members of Parliament appeared to be very callous on the subject, and the remnant who would not bow the knee to Baal not only incurred a great deal of abuse, but were also from time to time impressed, like himself, with the despairinenature of the struggle. There seemed to be a kind ef determination—an invincible resolution— en the part of the majority of the members of the House of Commons either to spend money recklessly or to sup- port such reckless expenditure. Subsequent dis- closures had borne him out that waste and extravagance were going on to an incredible extent. He described the present system as having been convicted before Parlia- ment and the people of being utterly rotten and bad, i and as having come to a crisis n which the Government were pledged to consider it with a view to reforms. It might be that to some extent and in some circumstances he would favour what was called a spirited foreign policy, wisely pursued, but it would be dangerous in the extreme to pursue such a policy under the present naval and military conditions of the country. For such a policy he would be sorry, to become in any way respon- sible. Sir Matthew White Ridley, M.P. Mr. Hanbury, M.P., and Mr. Tomlinson, Biz, also addressed the meeting.

div.p: and-water. And here comes in the saddest part of my story, sir, for we are poor, like thousands and thousands of families in these great factory towns, and couldn't afford to let our hard-earned money go for nothing. And yet- -and yet," here the poor woman struggled with emotion, "when I think how we had worn out all our savings on the doctors and their medi- cines, and I kept on sinking all the time, and we poorer and poorer- -why, I just can't bear the thought of it."
Here she broke down, and cried bitterly at the mere recollection of what she had gone through.

Her visitor wiped the moisture from his own eyes, and comforted her by. saying, "Don't mind it. That is all gone by, and your health is now re- stored. Tell me how you got well, and forget the gloomy past." Cheering up at these words, she added: "That I will gladly, sir, for it is a. short, plain story to tell, It was at Easter, in the year 1882, I was so bad that, unless I was to get better, I did not care if I didn't live to hear the bells ring at Christmas, for what is the use of living if one is to be always ill and unhappy ? It was then, sir, that Mr. Booth, of Waterhead, or Mrs. Cox, of the same place (I won't be sure which now, sir), recommended me to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I was afraid to spend the money for fear I should be deceived again, but I bought a bottle for all that, and, you may not believe me, but I felt better after the first five or six doses. My food stopped on my stomach, there was no more burning inside, my head got clear, and all those bad signs I spoke of began to abate. I didn't get well all at once, but after I had taken five bottles of the Syrup I felt as if I was made over again, and the past twenty years of pain and illness was only a bad dream. That is five years ago now, sir, and the terrible old trouble has never come back."
Both Mrs. Gartside and her husband, express their thanks to God for her recovery, and give all praise to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup as the only medicine that did her the slightest good.

Note.- -The "burn canful " to which Mrs. G. refers is a large can with handles, in which water is carried from the wells, and is a familiar expression in the Oldham district to denote a large quantity. Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup is for sale by all chemists and medicine vendors, and by the proprietors, A. J. White, Limited, 35, Farringdon-road, London, E.C. Price 2s. 6d. per bottle.

div.head: Ettttr to tbe Obitor. THE LICENSING CLAUSES-COMPENSATION.
div.p: Ettttr to tbe Obitor. THE LICENSING CLAUSES-COMPENSATION.
Sir,-
"lie wot takes wot isn't his'n,

Wi-ren.'h-e's—cotched he goes to Prison." 'his by the way, and as a warning to dishonest people. From boyhood I have been in the habit of attending various places of worship, Church of England, Noncon- formist, Roman Catholic, Unitarian, and even Agnostic, and have heard it universally, taught, that if one man deprived another of that which was his own, that he— the depriver—was a thief. Similarly, if I were on a County Council, as proposed by the present Government and by my casting vote, turned a publican out of his house, and thus robbed his family of their daily bread, should regard myself as an unmitigated scoundrel, and as deserving a thief's fate, and in my humble opinion, whoever else perpetrates this offence, either by word or deed, is just as bad as I should be under the same cir- cumstances; and no amount of "Local Option" sophis- try, or any other pious fraud on his own conscience can get him out of it. The plunderers—and there are many who virtually advertise themselves as such—may say they won't steal, they will only stop a legitimate sale; which is exactly what the Fox said when he ran away with the Duck, to prevent it's feeding some other animal rather than himself.
" Sez John C. Calthoun, sez he— Human rights haint no more Right to come on this floor, No more'n the man in the moon,' sez he." BELLEROPHON.
Warrington, 17,5, 1888.
MINE RENTS AND MINERAL ROYALTIES..-NO 2.

Sir,—lt is often very difficult to give a precise mean- ing to a word which is used by so many people in dif- ferent senses, but if I might be allowed to venture for a moment on the hazardous ground of definition, I should say that a "good and robust Radical," as Mr. Percy puts it, is a man who could, with a full appreciation of the meaning of the words, subscribe to the passage I quoted last week, from Professor Jevon's book on "The State in Relation to Labour." That passage, again, is but an _ . _ . .

. • • amplification of the old Latin motto, " Salus populi -suprema lex "—the good or welfare of the people or State is the supreme law. Radicals are sometimes charged with being the advocates of "confiscation." that is the taking away of people's property without full compensa- tion. I should say, however, that a Radical neither repudiates nor accepts confiscation as a part of his politi- cal methods. "Is it for the good or welfare of the State that this thing should be done or left undone ? " is the first question whicho a sound Radical will put to himself in regard to any political question or proposal. If in his opinion it is better that it be done, then he considers the mode of doing it. This is a matter of pure expediency— of "adjustment and compromise." If the reform can only be carried out, or can best be carried out—always having a view to the public good—by what is called • "confiscation," that a Radical, I should think, can have no hesitation as to the course that ought to be taken. He does not admit that there is any "absolute right" to property. He holds with Professor Jevons that "no rights of property are so sacred that they may not be done away with if it can be clearly shown that they stand in the way of the greatest happiness." The sole justification of private property is the public good; when that justification is shown not to exist, private property should cease to exist also. But, on the other hand, when it can be shown on a balance of argument that a reform canbe carried out most expediently by full or partial com- pensation, I do not think that the extremist Radical would for a moment advocate "confiscation." Now, this is an attitude essentially different from that which Mr. Percy takes up with regard to mineral royal- ties. He says that at some time past "the nation gave away all its minerals," and that therefore he would "not confiscate a single pound of coal and iron." Once let the advocates of reform concede all that is implied in this sentence, and we may say farewell to all hopes of • advancement and improvement. They would thereby turn their backs upon the great principle that mere pn- Tate and sectional privileges must make way for the advancement of the public good, and they would admit that there was something so sacred about private pro- perty that it could net be touched without the amplest • compensation. But progress and compensation are sometimes utterly incompatible with each other, and if you admit the latter you stop the former. Take the case of mechanical improvement. During the last fifty years how many thousands of working-men have been thrown out of employment by the introduction of improved ma- chinery ? In numberless instances these workmen have spent many of the best years of their life in acquiring a skill in workmanship by the exercise of which they ex- pected to earn a comfortable livelihood, but suddenly machinery is introduced which entirely supersedes their skill, and they are either left without employment or forced down into the ranks of common and ill-paid labour. Here is " confiscation "of property which is as real and-as much a source of profit and as much sanc- tioned by the law as land and minerals or brick and mor- tar, and yet we never hear any cries for cempensation from the " expropriated " workmen. If such a cry were raised, what would be the argument used against it? Would it not be that to grant compensation to aisplaced workmen would be to stop all mechanical progress, because no manufacturer could afford to set up new machinery if he had to fully com- pensate all the workmen it displaced? What reason is there then that we should be more in- dulgent to the rich royalty receiver than to the poor artizan P There is a political progress to be stopped as well as mechanical progress. If, in order to allow of this political progress, it be necessary for royalty receivers to give way, let them give way as workmen do in the case of new machinery, and do not let us talk as though the State had "given away" all its minerals beyond the right or possibility of recovery.—l am, PHYSIOCRAT.

RECH4.1311% DEMONSTRATION AT KINGSLEY.—On Tues- day afternoon the annual festival in connection with the "Hope of Kingsley" Tent, No. 214, Winsford unity, took place. The members, to the number of upward S of 200, started in procession from the Wesleyan schoolroom, heaxl3d by the Overton Bible Class and the Northwich Blue Ribbon Army brass bands. The procession, after having made the circuit of the principal residents in the • neighbourhood, returned to the schoolroom, where a pub- lic tea was provided, the rest of the evening being spent in an enjoyable way. METHODIST FREE CHURCH: RE-OPENING SERVICES.— `This church, having been closed for painting; and reno- vation, was re-opened on Sunday, when special sermons were preached, in the morning by the Rev. W. R. Mul- let, circuit minister, and in the afternoon and evening by Mr. J. Toogood, of Helsby. There was a good attendance at each service. On Monday afternoon a tea was provided in the schoolroom, and was well patron- ised. In the evening a public meeting was held in the chapel, when addresses were delivered by the Revs. E. Hall (Runcorn), G. Rennison (Frodsham Primitive Methodists), W. R. Mullett (Frodsham), and Mr. Scott. Mr. A. White, of Helsby, presided. It is believed that he proceeds of these services, together with previous rts, will defray the whole expense of renovating and 'fling the chapel. The usual votes of thanks very pleasant evening to a close.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hal on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. T. S. Timmis, J P., pre- sided, and there were present the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, Messrs. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., R. Bradshaw, R. H. Davies, F. Heyes, G. H. Denby (clerk.)

I -THE HOLIDAYS. The School Management Committee reported that they had arranged that the holidays at the schools this year should be as follows :—Whit week and three weeks at Midsummer, commencing at noon on Friday June 29th, and ending on the morning of Monday July 23rd.—Dean Finegan moved the adoption of this minute, and said the managers of the various schools would agre• to this arrangement .—The minute was passed.

div.head: 'THE CLERKS IN CONFERENCE : THE EXPENSE.
div.p: 'THE CLERKS IN CONFERENCE : THE EXPENSE.

The Finance Committee also reported that they had authorised the Clerk to the Board to attend the confer- ence of School Board Clerks in Edinburgh from the 23rd to the 26th may.—Dr. O'Keeffe, in moving the adoption of this minute, said the committee also recommended that the clerk's expenses be paid.—ln reply to the chair- man, Mr. Danby said the conference was an annual one, and he had been in the habit of attending it for some years. He had never yet had his expenses paid.—The Chairman thought it desirable that the clerk should at- tend the conference, as there was a great deal of valuable information as to the working of School Boards to be gained. He was also of opinion that his expenses should be paid.—Dean Finegan asked what guarantee had they that Mr. Danby represented the Board. He should ob- ject to Mr. Danby speaking on behalf of the Board unless the members had held a meeting on the subject before he went—Mr. Deacon was stronglv of opinion that the Board ought not to pay Mr. Danby's expenses unless he went to say what the Board told him.—Dr. O'Keeffe said there was an official of high position on the Local Board who attended a conference of engineers. The members I of the Board were not engineers, and he could not repre- sent their views ; therefore he to a great extent represen- ted himself ; but he brought back valuable information for the benefit of the Board.—The Clerk read the pro- gramme of the conference, from which it appeared that papers were read on various subjects connected with education, and discussions took place.—Ultimately the minute was altered to read "That the request of the clerk to attend the conference of School Board clerks be granted," and was passed. The question of expenses was left open.

div.head: THR RATE OF INTEREST ON LOANS.
div.p: THR RATE OF INTEREST ON LOANS.

TheFinanceCommittee recommended that the Board be empowered to obtain a Loan of £4OOO from the Public Works Loan Commissioners, for the additional accom- modation required at the Simm's Cross, Warrington-road, and West Bank Schools' and the necessary furniture and fittings, for 30 years at 34 per cent. The Clerk said in accordance with the direction of the Board, he on the 25th April addressed the following letter to the Public Works Loan Board:—" In order to carry out school ex- tensions the Education Department have sanctioned my Board borrowing £4OOO from your Board, the repayment to be spread over 30 years. I am desired to ask what rate the Public Works Loan Board will require under the conditions referred to. As the Government are now a,ble to borrow money on reduced terms, it is assumed by my Board that the rate charged on loans for public purposes will be reduced to the same extent." In reply the Public Works Loan Board merely stated that in the event of a loan being granted repayment within a period of 30 years, the rate of interest would be 34 per cent. On the 27th April Mr. Hanby acknowledged this letter, and added: "Before replying further my Board will be glad to have reply to the question raised in the last paragraph of my letter of the 25th instant." A reply was received on the 30th April, informing the Board that the rate of interest on the Public Works Board's loans was not affected by the financial proposals referred to in the last paragraph of Mr. Danby's letter. —The Chairman said it came to this: they might borrow the money on the Loan Commissioners terms or go with- out. He suggested that the terms be accepted. He be- lieved the rate of interest would be reduced by and bye, and the reduction made retrospective.—Major Wareing said they could borrow money from many sources on I better terms. The recommendation Was referred back for further consideration.

div.head: REV. G. BOND RESTON&
div.p: THE REV. G. BOND RESTON&
The Clerk read a letter from the Rev. G. Bond, recen- tly vicar of Farnworth, resigning his position as a mem- ber of the Board.—On the proposition of the Cnairman the resignation was accepted.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of the Run- corn Football Club was held at Wilson's Hotel on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. R Filth, the president occupied the chair, and there was an excel- lent attendance. Amongst those present were, Dr. Mangan, Messrs. Jesse Timmins, H. Wright, W. Carroll, John Lunt, William Riley, T. E. Booth, A. Riley, S. H. Dawson, W. Frith, W. Wright, T. Clegg, Thomas Moores, W. Hughes, H. Hughes, J. Gatley, G. Wainwright, J. Clarke, R. Moores, J. E. Lang- sbaw (secretary), C. Pownall (treasurer).

SECRETARY'S REPORT. The Secretary read his report, which stated that the first team had played 33 matches, of which 17 were won, 9 lost, and 6 drawn. The total score was 26 goals, 36 tries, and 128 minor points, against 11 goals, 21 tries, and 54 minor points. There was a difference in favour of Runcorn of 15 goals, 15 tries, and 74 minors. Tries were obtained as follows :—Wainwright 7, Speakman 7, Hugh Hughes 6, Broady 5, Faulkner 5, W. A. Riley 4, Davies 3, Whitby 3, and Wright, P. Riley, Stubbs, Gay- ter, and W. Hughes two each. T. Davies dropped two goals, and Speakman, T. Woods, and Hughes dropped one goal each. Woods kicked 12 goals out of 26 attempts; Brazendale kicked 9 goals out of 22 attempts; and Broady had 6, Hughes 2, and Speakman 1 attempts,, but failed in all. The second team " had played at matches, had won 18, lost 5, and drawn 3. Their aggre- gate score was 25 goals, 33 tries, and 103 minor points, against their opponents 4 goals, 17 tries, and 33 minors; a majority in favour of Runcorn of 21 goals, 16 tries, and 70 minor points.
TRE tSIITRER'S REPORT.

The Treasurer read a statement of accounts from which it appeared that the club commenced the season with a balance in hand of £59 16s 10d, and amongst the amounts received were—lion. members' subscriptions, £44 us 6d; ordinary members', £lB 16s 6d; ladies' season tickets, £6 17s 8d; gate receipts, £5OO 17s 6d. The total receipts was £B4l 8s 7d. After paying all ex- penses there was a balance in hand of £8 12s 10d.—The reports were adopted on the motion of Mr. W. Riley, seconded by Mr. W. Massey.

MR. FRITH RETIRES.—TRE NEW PRESIDENT. The Chairman said it afforded him great pleasure to meet them on that annual occasion, and to find that the club had been so successful during the past year. He only trusted that the same good fortune,which depended upon the energy of members, would attend upon the club next season. Not long ago a Liverpool gentleman told him that Runcorn had got to the front by good ster- ling hard work. When he became their president he little thought that Runcorn was going to shine in the brilliant manner that they had done, and on his retire- ment from that position he felt gratified that they had achieved so noble a reputation.—For the position of president Major Hazlehurst and Mr. S. Taylor were nominated, and the former gentleman was elected by 52 votes to 35.—Mr. W. Wright proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Frith for his. past services.—Mr. T. Clegg seconded the proposition, which, was carried enthusiasti- cally, and the Chairman suitably responded'.

div.head: OFFICERS..
div.p: THE OFFICERS..

The Chairman announced that Mr. It Hughes had I been unanimously elected as captain of the first team, and in flattering terms he proposed a vote of thanks to that player.—Mr. W. Wright seconded the proposition, which was carried with loud acclamation.—The captain suit- ably responded.—Mr. J. E. Langshaw was unanimously re-elected secretary at a salary of £lO per annum, and Mr. C. Pownall was also unanimously re-elected treasurer at a salary of £7 per annum. These officers were cor- dially thanked for their past labours, as was also Mr. Alfred Riley, the assistant secretary. Mr. G. Wain- wright was appointed vice-captain by 68. votes. Mr. John Gatley was unaninsously appointed captain of the second team, and Mr. J. H. Crompton subcaptain. Mr. W. Wright was appointed umpire of the first team by 80 votes to Mr. H. G. Andrews 15 votes. Mr. W. Dun- , bavand was appointed umpire to the, second team. Messrs. W. Massey and E. Kay were appointed the audi- tors.
THE CONAIITTIIE,

There were 22 nominations for 12 seats on the commit- tee and the following gentlemen were elected :—W. Hughes, 83 votes; James Clarke, 71; W. Faulkner, 70; T. Morris, 87; T. E. Booth, 69; John. Lunt, 64; Thos. Clarke, 61; W. Carroll, 60; H. G. Andrews, 82; W. H. Broady, 54; William Riley, 51; Thoma-s Whinyates, 51. On the proposition of Dr. Mangan, seconded by Mr. Gat- ley, the retiring committee were heartily thanked for their labours in the past.

div.head: TH3e HONORARY PHYSICIAN.
div.p: TH3e HONORARY PHYSICIAN.

The Chairman, in eulogistic ten-r.;, proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. Mangan, the honorary physician, for his valuable services during the past year. Mr. H. Hughes, tile captain, seconded the resolution. Dr. Mangan, he said, was always at hand when any emergency occurred.—The motion was carried with great enthusiasm, and Dr. Mangan acknowledged the compliment.
NEXT SEASON.

The Chairman announced that matches had been ar- ranged for next mason with Salford, Bradford, Kendal Hornets, Leeds St. Johns, Broughton Rangers, Rochdale Hornets, Eirkenkead Park, Liverpool Old Boys, New Brighton, Owens College, Sale, Stockport, Manchester Rangers, Burton-on-Trent, Oldham, and Manchester Free Wanderers. Other matches were in course of arrange- ment.
CONCLI7SION.

The customary votes -4 thanks brought the proceed- ings to a close. The business wastrausacted with greater dispatch than usual, through an improved system of voting by ballot that had been adopted. The tellers, Messrs E. Kay, W. Maass'', and S. H. Dawson, ably per- formed their duties.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1888.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) WESTON. Operations on this section are still confined to the work of preparation. The joiners and blacksmiths are kept busily employed each day in constructing necessary ar- ticles that will be skilfully and powerfully used ere long. For :nstance, two pile drivers have been fitted up, and a third is under way, but in consequence of the interfer- ence of the Mersey. Conservancy Board they are yet lying idle. On the Weaver wharf thousands of piles are I stacked, and some hundreds are prepared ready for piercing the bed of the Mersey. Of the latter, some have a wedge-shaped end, which is protected viith iron, whilst others are brought to a point, also encased with iron. The piles are about 30 feet long. As yet only two out of the six navvy's houses that are to be erected on the wharf have been occupied, but there are indica- tions that the remainder will not be long wanting ten- ants. A quarter of a mile away, at the Runcorn end of the docks, other houses are in course of erection by Mr. T. Kirkham's workmen, and will be quickly com- pleted. A short line of railway metals have also been laid along the river side from the line which runs to Runcorn Docks, to the docks at Weston Point. RUNCORN. On this section work is proceeding briskly. The amount of toil and clay that is removed daily is some- thing enorettous. At the Big Field, Norton, the three Priestman's grabs are proving a great success. One of these grabs is supposed to be doing its duty if it fills 80 waggons per day, equal to about 340 tons of soil, but those in use are daily filling no less than 120 waggons. Nearer Runcorn the American navvies are forging ahead in grand style. Two of the uncanny looking monsters are engaged in lengthening the cutting, whilst a third is making it the necessary width. At present there is a gorgemearly three quarters of a mile in length, 20 feet deep, and at one part nearly 150 feet wide. The steam navvy at work above the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele has also succeeded in making a deep cutting several hundred feet in length. Considerable difficulty s still experienced in laying the spoil bank on the marsh at Norton. As the thousands of tons of material are de- posited each day, the ground sinks two or three feet lower beneath the tremendous weight, and great care and watchfulness is required to pre- vent disaster. The trial holes sunk in the land near the Old Quay Works have revealed rock about 20 feet bendath the surface, and no doubt this fact will be hailed with satisfaction by Mr. Walker, as a large quantity of stone will be required in the con- struction of the estuary. On Wednesday telephonic communication was established between Manchester and the offices at the Old Quay Docks, Runcorn, and all the intermediate depots. In a short time the wires Will be extended to Weston Point and thence on to Eastham. This is another evidence of the completeness of Mr. Wal- ker's arrangements for carrying, out his gigantic under- taking. In consequence of Whitsuntide the men will stop work on Saturday at noon, and will not resume until Wednesday morning. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. On Tuesday, a navvy employed on the Ship Canal works, whose name is Robert Woods, and who lives at Runcorn, was admitted to the Warrington Infirmary suffering from a compound fracture of the leg, caused by a quantity of soil falling upon him. He is progress- ing as favourably as can be expected. WALTON, MOORE, Sze. On making a visit to Acton Grange and Moore, this week, it was easily to be seen that considerable progress continues to be made in the work of construction in that neighbourhood. A steam navvy of the American type is in full swing on the ground a little beyond Morley Com- mon and a visitor standing on the arches at Walton and looking in that direction now views a very bustling scene. It is only recently that operations were commenced in that immediate locality, but a long cutting has already been made by the navvy. A second steam navvy is on the ground here, and at the time of our visit it was being prepared for use. Surface earth is being removed, and offices and various wooden buildings are mak- ing their appearance in all directions. Among them is a very long row of workmen's cottages. One or two of them are already occupied, and they have a very neat and homely appearance. The others are apparently ready for occupation. The cutting further On in the direction of Moore is also assuming larger pro- platen.% and the locomotives are kept busy all day long carrying away the excavated material. In one part of this cutting there is a quantity of red, clay-like soil, and, there being also a good deal of water in the bottom iof the cutting, it s a matter of inconvenient labour to remove the mixture. For this purpose, several large scoops, similar in shape to the ones used in the work of the steam navvy, but without the "teeth," are placed on the ground. They are then filled by means of the spade and as each one receives its complement it is lifted 'up by a steam crane, swung round to a position immediately over one of the train waggons, into which the soil is then tipped. Though, of course, thisis a more Itedious process than that of filtingthe waggons by means of tfie " navvy," it is surprising with what despatch a train is loaded. The building of another lot of cottages has been completed about a mile distant from the village of Moore, and a large place to be used as a refreslinient room is also finished.

ACCIDENT AT STATHAM. On Monday last a man known by the name of Big John" met with a serious accident on the Ship Canal at Statham. It appears that his duty was to replace the waggon on its wheels alter the locomotive had grren it a knock to throw it up and tip the clay out. After he got the waggon all right, he gave the order to the engine driver before he was clear of the line, and the wheel of the waggon passed over his leg, badly fracturing it. Drs. Williamson aud his brother were soon in attendance, and afterwards the patient was removed to a wooden house Thelwall, until the hospital, which is being built in that neighbourhood, is ready. LYMM. There is little progress to report with regard to,the section of the canal at Statham. It is stated that nego- tiations are still being carried on with the landowners, and in the meantime the new steam navvy which has been erected standsidle, facing on of the road ways in this direction which it is proposed to intersect- Most care seems to be directed to pumping operations at this part of the canal just now. A powerful pulsoineter is engaged in draining the field to the west of the late sew- age farm, and nearer to the river two ordinary suction pumps are being worked by manual labour. Away in the direction of Thelwall a number of workmen were yesterday afternoon engaged in puttingup another steam navvy of what is popularly known as the " American " type:

some important modification had been made in regard to this matter. He thought that the resolution was a fair one, because it did not commit the meeting to an expression of opinion as to whether or not compensation should be given in the matter of taking away licenses. It simply requested the with- drawal of the licensing clauses. He, for one, contended that it would be better to deal with the licensing ques- tion in a separate measure altogether, and he thought that they would then have a far much better chanc* of an equitable arrangement being arrived at. The dual control of the police, and the proposed ex- officio representation upon county councils, would be most unfair. He could not understand why, in a matter of that sort, they were afraid to appeal to the people. If they desired a just representation, there was no reasodwhy they should not adopt the same principle as that adopted in the present mode of election to Parlia- ment. Why should it be possible for the aristocracy to ensure a certain number on the County CouncihsHe had heard much expression of opinion lately in regard to the bill, and he had heard ' enthusiastic Conservatives in Warrington express themselves as totally opposed to the licensing clauses. As regarded vested interests, he mentioned the recent extension of Bridge-street for Corporation improvements. Ptople had shops in that street who had spent a lifetime in establishing a good business. What compensation did the Corporation offer them ?' Not a halfpenny piece. They simply had to accept the usual notice to leave their shops. He happened to know of one or two instances where the tenants were not in a position to buy the expensive land, were unable to build other pre- mises, and had suffered most ternbly. The case of sr publican was not so unjust as that, because it was well understood that a publican's license was granted for twelve months, and for twelve months only, and that, if the magistrates thought proper, the license could be re- fused at the end of that time. He hoped that the whole' strength of the Liberal party would be raised against these licensing propositions, and that they would be. withdrawn. (Applause.)

The CHAIRMAN expressed himself as in, agreement with. Mr. Walker in regard to the compensation clauses. He held the opinion that there was no. money value in licenses, which were clearly under the control of the jus- tices. Rethought, however, that a question like the exten- sion of Btidge-st., referred to by Mr. Roberts, had nothing to do with the matter at all. A lluidlord could turn out a tenant at a given notice,. and if, in conse— quence of street improvements, a tenant was turnetl out before his notice had expired he got compensation for it. The public-house had a compensation title.a.s.a building merely, but there should be no compensation madewith., regard to licenses. He also pointed out that in the elec- tion to County Councils the rich would have no power over the poor. The representation was on the same lines as our Town Councils. A County Council would have power within itself to select members, and this Mt. Walker objected to; but only the' representatives them- selves could vote for these selected ones, just in the same. way as a Town Council selected aldermen. (Applause.) Mr. W. RORMRTS l said that, if the publican had a, right to compensation, the tradesmanhad a greaterright. (Hear, hear.) . _

„ , Mr. S. lhatow wished to impress upon his teetotal friends that they should not be so,intemperate in their castigation, He wished also to say that he *greed en- tirely with the preposition, except the last clause. Ho did not believe in aldermanie supervision at all, and he thought that aldermen were &curse to municipal go- vernment He did not think that the course that the , Liberal party proposed to take.iii reference to the publi- cans was a proper one. He thought that, in spite of the legal authority that had been quoted to the contrary, I there was a vested interest to be considered. It was, amongst sensible and, business men, an understood thing that when a person rented or bought a public-house the license was of very great value. If ahouse was iin4-1 properly conducted, the person holding the license should, of course, forfeit 'it. Public-houses were going down in value—(hear, hear,)—and' he believed' that before long many of them, would have to be shut I up by force of circumstances, because they could not pay their way. Mr. E. Ptaismv expressed himself as being entirely in accord with the terms of the resolution, and remarked as touching upon the-licensing portion of the measure, that the other week, in Warrington, a man was turned' out of a licensed house at a moment's notice, and got no. compensation whatever. If the compensation clause' was passed, most of the money would go to the large brewers. He scarcely thought that the bill would pass at all; it was too radical in. some respects and too conservative in others.

Mr, WALKER replying to Mr. Barlow, said that he was prepared to admit that there was an impression amongst brewem and publicans that there was a vested interest in licenses, but the Court of Queen's Bench had given a decision to the contrary. Mr. Gladstone too, had stated that there was no vested interest in a licence. The resolution was then carried unanimously, and it was further decided that copies of it be forwarded to Mr. Gladstone, Mr. W. S. Caine, Mr. Ritchie, and Lord Salisbury. Dr. GORNALL proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Walker for having introduced the discussion. Referring .to the compensation clauses, he • said he thought that if the Liberal party took the matter up they would appeal with success to the ratepayers of the country, and do some- thing towards ousting the present government from of- fice. The sooner that was done; the better. (Hear, hear.) . . . .
The proposition, which was- seconded by Mr. William Rommrs; was cordially c,arried, and the proceed- ings then terminated with the passing of a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday evening a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Warrington Liberal Association was held at the Liberal Club in Bewsey-et., the principal object for which it was cal'ed being to consider the provisions of the bill brought in. by the Government in the House of Commons in regard to Local Government, Mr. J. Walker baying engaged to introduce the subject. The chair was occupied by Councillor F. A. Roberts, and amongst those also present wen° Councillors W. Pierpoint and J. H. Fleming, Dr. Gornall, Messrs. J. Walker, John Harrison, William Roberts, S. Barlow, N. Legge, Kiernan, J. Clayton (Liberal agent), and others. After formal business had been disposed of, Mr. Joun WALKEa introduced the subject of the Local Government Bill, in regard to which discussion was invited. He said that the bill was practically a revolution in. local government, and it was one, so far as he could judge, that had not been discussed one-tenth as much as it should be. On the face of it, the bill seemed to be one that was broad and democratic in its lines, but when it came to be examined one found that a good deal of the democracy disappeared —that there was a giving with one hand and a tak- ing sway with the other. (Applause.) He should touch upon some of the leading principles of the measure, to show how far they were in° accord with what they conceived to be Liberal principles and how far they as a party could give these main por- tions of the bill their support. The financial proposals in themselves formed a vast subject for discussion, and were open to criti- cism.. There was one feature that especially interested Warrington at the present moment—the pos- sibility of Warrington coming to be a town-county. A. poll had been taken during the week with the view of seeing how near the population came to the magical number of 50,000. If this proposal regarding tewn- counties became law, Warrington might, after all, be left out in the cold, as a town-county. It would remain in the county of Lancaster as at present. That would mean that Warrington would occupy an unsatisfactory posi- • tion. In the first place, it would have less power of self- government than the town-counties, and in the second place there would be an added burden in the shape of contribution to county rates. It was laudable for towns like Warrington to endeavour to get made into town- counties, but the point suggested another matter,. As- suming that the smaller towns were included'as counties, how would it stand with the rural and semi-rural population in Lancashire? If there was a burden it would be increased by having numbers of towns in Lan- cashire made into town-counties. That being the case, he could not but feel that, if it should end in that, a great injustice would be done to the rural population, and his opinion was that a bill which, by its very framing and inception, inevitably led to that position, was on the face of it a bad one. They did not wish a bill to be brought forward that would make bad worse; they wanted one that would make bad better. The rural population would have fair right to cry out against the bill, if they had an addition made in consequence to their county rates. (Hear, hear.) He now wished to speak to, and would propose the adoption of, the follow- ing resolution :

That this meeting of the Executive of the Warrington Liberal Association, while regarding with satisfaction the pro- posal to establish county government on the haais of a demo- cratic suffrage, under the protection of the ballot, disapproves of the provision for iatroducing a proportion of " selected " representatives; believds that the proposal to establish dual control in the management of the county police is subversive of the principles of representative government; and urges that the licensing and compensation clauses should be with- drawn, as contrary to the letter and spirit of previous legisla- tion, and calculated to lay a burden upon the backs of the people too grievous to be borne. (Applause.)

With regard to the first point in the resolution—selected representatives—the assumption was that they were go- ing to have county government on the same lines as were laid down in regard to boroughs. It was really a question of introducing aldermen in local county govern- ment, an element which he considered to be a bad one. The system of selected representatives was a bad system; the very word "selected" was in itself invidious. They wanted representatives, not selected from the ratepayers but elected by the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) Another sop to the upper classes lay in the provision that the chairnian of a County Councilmust be qualified to be a justice of the peace. Could they not conceive of a clear-headed, intelligent man who had no aspiration to be a justice of the peace, who would still be capable of being a good chairman of a County Council? Such a provision was a slur upon the capa- city of the Council, and on the ratepayers generally. No qualification was insisted upon in regard to a member of Parliament, or even a Prime Minister, and he pro- tested against the absurdity of such a qualification being made in regard to County Councils. The justices, he found, were to have powers that weye administrative, which, he thought, should be left entirely to the County Council. For instance, what should be the assessment committee of the County Council would not have the power of assessing property without the justices of the peace in Quarter Sessions having a singer in the pie. Let the justices be justices ; let them keep to their judicial function, and not go beyond it. Perhaps the reason was that these gentlemen had been in the habit of settling the basis of assessment very much as they liked, and in favour of their mansions and parks, as compared with other property and they were still to have this improper authority.. The provisions withregard to the dual control of the police were also bad. The County Council had not even: the power of electing a Chief Constable—a power that many a small borough had enjoyed for something like fifty years. This was prepos- terous. A provision was alai made that the County Con- stabulary should be managed by. a joint committee of the Quarter Sessions and the County Council, which was merely another sop to the magistrates. Power was given to County Councils to close public-houses on Sundays, Christmas Days; and Good Fridays. If it was legitimate to close them one day in the week without compensation, why should it not be legitimate to close them altogether? If there was a claim for compensation at all, it held good with regard to the days mentioned. The fact that it was ignored in regard to Sundays, Christmas Days, and Good Fridays, was an acknowledgment by publi- cans, that they did not conceive that they had what they regarded as a good, solid claim, Provision was ' alsornade by which people living near a licensed house !could endeavour to make out a case against such house, in order that the license might be cancelled. That provision was a good one, and one to which they could not, on the face of it, object, but there was the draw- back—that if the justices decided that the application should be dismissed there was then an end of the matter. But, on the other hand, if a brewer or a publican ap- peared before the justices, and they decided that a case .had been made out for cancellingthe license, the brewer, ;or' publiiign, had power to appeal to the Quarter See- ' sions. That an appeal should be denied to one person ,and given to another was, the speaker urged, an inips- dice, and one that should be stremunisly opposed by the "Liberal party. Then, again, there was the question of compensation fot licenses. Mr Caine, M.P., had gene into this subject, and had found that on an average the groposed compensation woul& arenunt to £3,000 for every license. That was an extraordinary sum for them to contemplate. Temperance reformers, and others who wished to deal with the drink traffic, wisuld stand aghast at such a psopofition. By it yir- tne would be handicapped, and vice would be given a free hand. Everything was done to make the way easy for " publicans and sinners," but very little appeared to be done in the way of watching the interests of the rate- payers. (Hear, hear.) If Warrington became a county, whenever money was to be paid for compensation, for the purchase of a license, it was-to be paid out o( the borough fund. He urged that the whole of the compen- sation clauses were objectionable from beginning to end. In Warrington, one penny inithe pound was estimated to bring in £540 per year, say £5OO roundly spectating. ' Putting the value of a license down at £2,000‘ which was £l,OOO less than the average given by Mr. Caine, it would require 4d in the on: the rates to get rid of one . license. But suppose the average value throughout the country was £l,OOO, or £l,lOO, which it would be at least. That meant, as to Warrington, that they would not be able to touch a single license inthcoway of doing away with it, and granting compensatien under the bill, without add- ing 2cl in the £to the rates. It was generally contended' that one house was sufficient for 1,000 people, but in Warrington there were 135 licensed houses of one sort or another, and there were 71 off-licenses in addition. Without considering off-licensee, it would require £270,000 at £2,000 each-to deal with those 135 houses. If the principle of compensation was admitted, he thought the off-license holders were entitled at any rate to some compensation. But were they prepared to face a possi- bility of this kind? He asked them, in view of a recent decision in the Court,of Queen's Bench, where the judge declared that magistrates had absolute-power to. refuse any license without compensation—se decision, which showed that there was no such thing as.a vested interest —if they were prepared to put the publicans in any better position than that in which they stood' at present? brewers and publicans wanted to 'protect themselves in case of losing, licenses, let them do, as workitg-men did with their Friendly and Assurance Societies. Let theint aid each other other out of their own funds. by forming a Compensation Assurance Association, and not seek to come upon the ratepayers? He held that to pass the compensation clauses as they stood would be a fraud upon the people-of this country, and a burden upon themselves and upon posterity. (Ap- plause.) Mr. IVirtrais ROBERTS seconded the resolution, and thanked Mr. Walker for the lucid way in which he had explained the provisions of the bill. If. considered that this question could be viewed entirely as a political one, and he, for one, did not for one moment speak as a tem- perance reformer that night, but as a Liberal. In his opinion, the compensation clauses alluded to were a mon- strous injustice to the community, and he could not for a moment conceive that they would in their present shape pass the Mouse of Commons. He was positive that before many days had pasted they would And that

div.head: TFIELWALL.
div.p: TFIELWALL.

Or of the most interasting operationsvarried on in the part of the canal near 'fhelwall is the excavating of the new bed for the river to be diverted into near Wildegrace farmhouse. The spectator standing at the west side of the cutting on the footpath which leads from Thelwall ferry can see a large number of navvies dawn at a con+, siderable depth in the new river bed, busgy, employed in the labour of excavation. In order to get the displaced- soil up the steep incline ou, to the top of the spoil heap some ingenious devices are resorted to. Strong planks, are placed at a very steep i and one may say a precipi- tous gradient, from the bottom of the cutting to the top of the spoil heap. So steep is the gradient that it would be utterly impossible- for a navy- to wheel a loaded barrow up,. and so, in order to give him i a lift, at each incline of planks a rope s worked through, a pulley; one end of the rope is attached to the handles of: each loaded barrow, and to ' the other end a horse is yoked. As soon as the horse is put in motion the barrow begins to glide up-the ascent, and all the navvy has to do is to hold the handles of the barrow. When the barrow-is emptied the navvy slides down the-plank, a too rapid descent being prevented by the pully rope. Another mode of raising spoil is by placing finwloadedbarrows on a kind of platform, which is then hoisted by machinery to the top of thespoil heap, and when the barrows are emptied they are again deposi- ted on the platform and bet down by the same means. A third mode of raising soi' from the future bed of the river is by means of anestremelylong crane which raises large iron buckets as soon as they are filled.. The crane 1 is used for the deeper cuttings. A steam pump is also kept in motion in orderto keep the cutting' dry. Be- tween Thelwall and Morris Brook the two steam navvies have already completsd the cutting of one length of several yards in width and are now pretty well advanced another length, and so much are they kept employed that the-harsh rattle of the chains as the emptied buckets are let down to be again -filled, at the side a the cutting, may, during working hours, almost continually be heard from the Thelwall-road. It may new be noticed that many et the first rowcf navvies' huts built in this locality- are occupied, and from the papers nailed on doors it would seem that many of the others have already beers allotted to tenants. The large building which has been- in course of erectionsfor a fortnight or three weeks past, on Thelwall-road, near Cedar Lawn' is new pretty near completion. It is, we understand, to be used as a hos- pital,„and, judging- from appearance, its dormitories will be comfortable and well-aired.

SUICIDE AFTER ATTEMPTED MURDER.—On Thursday morning, Thomas Cox, a butcher, of Stapleton-road, during an altercation with his wife seized a chopper from a block, and alined a blow at her head. The woman, in protecting her head, received shocking in- juries to her arm but she managed to get away, and ran to the police station for assistance. On her return to the house with a constable, the husband was missing, and was subsequently found hanging to a beam in the slaughtor-house quite dead.

COPENITAGEN. FRIDAY'. The Danish Exhibition was opened to-day by the Xing, who was accompanied by members of the royal family, the ceremony being favoured by magnifiaent weather. THE EMPEROR FREDERICK, The following butietin was issued on Friday morning: The Emperor has been quite free from fever during the past few days,, and the difficulty in swallowing has entirely disappeared. The general condition is now so satisfactory that his Majesty spends the greater part of the day in the c,pen air. The illustrious patient's strength is visibly increasing, and there is less secretion."

THI9: WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS.

Plenty of. attractions are held out for tourists and others to enjoy themselves away from home during the Whitsuntide holidays. Messrs. James Little and Co. furnish details in another column of the Barrow route to the Isle of Man, which has the merit of affording the shortest sea passage. A train in con- nection with the steamers leaves Warrington (L. and N.W.R.) at 9-57 a.m. It will be seen, too, that the Cheshire Eines Committee have several trips on. Provision is made for those who are going to the Isle of Man having free conveyance of luggage across Liverpool until further notice. Passengers are also to be permitted to break the journey in Liverpool both going and returning. Cheap tickets are also being issued by the Cheshire Lines Committee for Manchester, on Whit-Monday, whilst to Liverpool and Southport there will be cheap fares every Saturday and Monday from to- day (Saturday) until further notice. The Great Western Railway Company are running excursion trains to-day and on Whit-Monday to Hereford, Tintern, Monmouth, and as far as New Milford; as well as to Oswestry, Shrewsbury, Llangollen, and Dolgelly. There are besides, on this line, three and five days' trips to almost every part of North Wales. Those who 'prefer excursions by sea are offered an opportunity by Messrs. R. and D. Jones, of Liver- pool', whose steamers leave Liverpool today and during the holidays, from the Prince s landing stage, for Llandudno, Beaurnaris,Bangor,and Menai Bridge. Particulars,are also given of steam communication between Liverpool and Glasgow, calling at Gree- nook. These steamers start from the Clarence Dock. Mr. David-,Macbrayne has special arrangements for summer tears in tho Highlands, the R.M.S. Col- umbwor lona sailing from Glasgow daily at 7 a.m., in connection with express trains from Warrington and the sotsth. The Zoological Gardens, Belle Vue, Manchester, will doubtless be well attendeo, as usual, as there are special attractions for the holi- days. The-firework spectacle, that has been pre- pared on e.,grand-scale, is a representation of the seige of Malta. For those who want to 'enjoy themselves a little nearer Home • the Belle Monte Pic-nie Grounds, lOverton Hill. Frodsharco will no doubt prove tempting. Visi- tors to the Ship Canal works, between Warring-. ton and Runcorn, are offered an opportunity ot obtaining, light refreshments at the Mersey Vale Refreshment Rooms, Moss-lane, Moore. It need hardly be said that there is a good opening for an establishment of this kind. It will be gathered from the details we have given, that if the pleasure seeker is troubled at all, it will be that he is embarassed with choice; but he can scarcely go wrong if thel weather continues fine, for the comp- try is beautiful at this time of the year.
