WHITSITNTIDE.—MT. W. H. &aim moved that the House at its rising should adjourn until the 31st May. LOCAL TAXATION IN SCOTLAND.—Oh this, motion Mr. Mimeses directed attention to the incidence of local taxation in Scotland, and the extent tb which it would be disturbed by the Budget proposals of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, respecting which he asked for infor- mation.—Dr. HUNTER said that the wheel tax was looked upon as an insult to the understanding of the people of Scotland.—Mr. MARX STEWART and Mr: EgSLF.MONT asked that the tax should not apply to Scotland—Mr. ISAACSON continued the discussion, but was called to,order for going into the general question of the wheel and van tax .-MrABRAHAMS inquiredabout the operation of the tax in Wales.—The CHANCELLOR of the Excnenutn, in reply, said that as regarded Wales, of course the Government would not maintain the tolls on turnpike roads if the wheel tax were applied to that country. With respect to Eno-land he had nothing to add to what he had pre- vious- said, namely, that the question whether the tax should or should not be imposed was not under his re- consideration. No doubt the owners of carts were against the tax, but there was a strong feeling in favour of it among those who would be benefited, and he was not prepared to withdraw the tax. He hoped; after .the House resumed, to give full particulars of the allowance the Government proposed to make to Scotland.— After some further debate the motion was carried unani- mously..

EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL. The debate on the motion for the second reading of the Employers' Liability Bill was resumed by Mr. FENwma. ,The bill was in some respects an improvement on the present /aye, but, looked at from workmen's point of view, it was not as satisfactory as the bill brought for- ward•by*Mr. Burt. 'He strongly condemned the provi- sionssof the bill which allowed parties to contract them- selves oat of the Act.—Mr. Tom/a/480N criticised the clauses in the bill, and Mr. GULLEY thought the bill unsatisfactory as regarded seamen and ship- owners. Mr. BRADLAUGH pointed out the ne- cessity of enlarging the compensation clauses. In the maim he approved of the proposal of the Govern- ment with regard to contracting out of the act, his be- lief 'being that there was a general feeling on the part of workmen in favour of a system of insurance which would sever them from the risk of a law sit.—Major Rascn,did not think the Bill provided for the protection of seamen'.,—Mr. DONALD CRAWFORD said he did not see why there should not be a system of insurance, with the right to fail back on the Employers' Liability Act:—The debate•w-as continued by Colonel Blundell, Mr. Abra- hams, Mi. C. Kenny, Admiral Field, Mr. Paulton, Mr. Pickersgill; and Mr. E. Spencer.—The Bill was then read a second time, and the committee was fixed for the 31st of May, when Mr. SMITH said, he would state whether it was to te•referred to the standing committee on trade or law.
The flOuse adjourned at ten minutes past six for the Whitsuntide holidays.

-, kr-f' RS. SARAH GARTSIDE resides at No. 7, Providence-street, Water- -47 F head, Oldham. Her husband, James Gartside, is employed as a - " piecer on upper mules," in the Bangor Mill, Oldham. Mrs. Gartside is a venerable and intelligent woman, now about 62 years of age. lier home is a model of neatness, and her visitor, whose call was wholly Unexpected, found her tidily dressed, as though she took an honest pride in her house and in herself. When asked to state the principal events in her remarkable experience, she responded very willingly, and what she said is here given practically in her own words :- -" I was always a healthy woman 1113 to the year 1862, but from that time on for twenty years I hardly saw a Well day, Ido not mean, sir, that I was laid up all that while, yet I was al- Ways ailing. My skin was mostly dry and hot, there was a bad taste in my inouth, and there would come a kind of wind or gas up from my stomach into my throat, which the doctors said was a sign of indigestion and clYspepsia. There was a scum on my teeth, my tongue would look coated or furred, too, and I noticed that more in the morning than at any other time Of the day. I had sick headaches a good deal, when it seemed I must go crazy with the pain and the dreadful feeling at the stomach. It would oirnetimes make me so blind, I could hardly see aught before my eyes. My skin was very yellow, which I was told came from the liver not acting, so that the bile was spread through the body and poisoned the blood. But What was worst, of all was the loss of appetite. Indeed, sir, that does not express it- -/ couldn't abide the sight of food. "I have gone a day and a night at a time without a morsel to eat, I was so afraid of it. It Beelned aS though if I should eat anything it would kill me on the spot. "The end of this was, sir, that I would be prostrated with weakness, and stay so for days together." Twenty years is a long time to suffer in that way, Mrs. Gartside," re- marked her visitor; "couldn't the doctors do anything for you P" "I have been treated by five of the best doctors in Oldham, but their skill Itailed to cure me. I have no fault to find with them, for they did all they ould for me, but they only relieve me for a little while; then the horrible trouble would be as strong as ever. Many's the time I felt it would be better to be dead than to lead such a life. But God's will be done. TVlty, sir, I have taken a burn canful of physic without any more benefit than so much sugar-
